topics.revision_note_md:
## Basics

- **Time complexity** = how the number of steps grows with input size *n*.
- **Space complexity** = extra memory you use (not counting the input).
- Drop constants and smaller terms: `3n² + 5n + 7` → **O(n²)**.
- Common orders: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ).
- **Rule of thumb:** ~10⁸ simple operations per second. n = 10⁵ → O(n²) is too slow, O(n log n) is fine.

lesson.simple:
Before learning any pattern, you need one skill: looking at code and saying **how slow it gets when the input grows**. That is Big-O.

Count the loops. One loop over *n* items is **O(n)**. A loop inside a loop is **O(n²)**. Halving the problem each step (like binary search) is **O(log n)**. Big-O ignores small details — `2n` and `n` are both O(n) — because for big inputs only the shape of growth matters.
lesson.analogy: Finding a friend in a stadium. Checking every seat one by one is O(n). If seats were sorted by name and you could jump to the middle and discard half each time, that's O(log n). Comparing every person with every other person (finding twins) is O(n²).

concepts.title: What Big-O actually measures
concepts.body:
Big-O describes **how the work grows as the input grows**, not how many milliseconds a program takes. If doubling the input roughly doubles the work, the algorithm is **O(n)**. If doubling the input makes it four times slower, it's **O(n²)**.

That's why we drop constants and smaller terms. Compare `3n² + 50n` and `n²` when n = 1,000,000: the `50n` part is 50 million, the `n²` part is a trillion. The small terms stop mattering, and so does the 3 — it only changes the speed by a fixed factor, not the *shape* of the growth.

Three cases people mix up:
- **Worst case** — the slowest input of size n. Interviews use this unless they say otherwise.
- **Average case** — expected time on typical input (quicksort: O(n log n) on average).
- **Amortised** — the average cost per operation over a long sequence. Appending to a Python list is O(1) amortised even though an occasional resize copies everything.

concepts.title: Counting the cost of code, line by line
concepts.body:
A reliable method for any snippet:

1. A simple statement (assignment, comparison, arithmetic, dict lookup) costs **O(1)**.
2. A loop costs **(number of iterations) × (cost of the body)**.
3. Code blocks one after another **add**: O(n) + O(n) = O(n).
4. Nested blocks **multiply**: a loop of n inside a loop of n is O(n²).
5. A loop where the variable is **multiplied or divided** each time (`i *= 2`, `n //= 2`) runs about **log n** times.

```python
for i in range(n):          # n times
    j = 1
    while j < n:            # log n times
        j *= 2
```
This is O(n log n). Watch for hidden loops: `x in some_list`, `list.index`, slicing `a[i:j]`, `s1 + s2` on strings and `sorted()` all cost more than O(1).

concepts.title: Space complexity and the recursion stack
concepts.body:
Space complexity counts the **extra memory** your algorithm needs on top of the input.

- A few variables → **O(1)**.
- A new list, set or dict that can grow with the input → **O(n)**.
- An n × m table → **O(n·m)**.

The one people forget is **recursion**. Each call that hasn't returned yet keeps a frame on the call stack. A recursive function that goes n levels deep uses **O(n) space** even if it creates no lists. Binary search written recursively uses O(log n) stack; written with a loop, O(1).

When an interviewer asks for *O(1) extra space*, they mean: modify the input in place (swaps, write pointers) and use only a fixed number of variables.

concepts.title: Reading constraints to pick the target complexity
concepts.body:
The constraint on n is a strong hint about the expected solution. A typical judge does around **10⁸ simple operations per second**:

| n up to | Target complexity | Typical idea |
|---|---|---|
| 10–12 | O(n!) | all permutations |
| 20–25 | O(2ⁿ) | all subsets, bitmask |
| 500 | O(n³) | triple loop, interval DP |
| 5,000 | O(n²) | pairs, 2D DP |
| 10⁵–10⁶ | O(n log n) or O(n) | sorting, heap, two pointers, hashing |
| 10⁹ and above | O(log n) or O(1) | binary search, maths |

So when you see n ≤ 10⁵, don't propose an O(n²) loop as your final answer. Say the brute force, then aim for O(n log n) or better.

concepts.title: The number tricks you'll reuse everywhere
concepts.body:
- **Digits:** `n % 10` gives the last digit, `n // 10` removes it. Loops over digits run O(log₁₀ n) times.
- **Divisors come in pairs:** if `d` divides `n`, so does `n / d`, and one of them is ≤ √n. So checking up to √n finds all divisors and tests primality in **O(√n)**.
- **GCD (Euclid):** `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b)`, ending when b = 0. It takes O(log min(a, b)) steps because the numbers shrink fast. `lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) × b`.
- **Sieve of Eratosthenes:** to find all primes up to n, cross out multiples of each prime starting at p × p. Total cost O(n log log n) — practically linear.
- **Modular arithmetic:** when an answer "may be large, return it modulo 10⁹+7", apply `% MOD` after every addition and multiplication so numbers stay small.

when_to_use: Every single interview question — you must state time and space complexity for your solution.
Deciding if a brute-force idea will pass: check the constraint on n first.
Digit tricks (`n % 10`, `n // 10`) show up in palindrome numbers, reversing integers, Armstrong numbers.
mistakes: Saying O(2n) or O(n + 5) — drop constants: it's O(n).
Forgetting space complexity: a new array of size n is O(n) extra space; recursion depth also counts.
Calling two separate loops O(n²) — sequential loops add (O(n + n) = O(n)); only nested loops multiply.
Integer overflow in other languages when reversing numbers — mention it even in Python.
interview_tips: Always say both: "Time O(n log n), extra space O(1)."
Read constraints first: n ≤ 10⁵ means you need O(n log n) or better.
For loops that halve (`i *= 2`, `n //= 2`), say O(log n) and explain why.

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of two nested loops, each running n times?
quiz.why: Nested loops multiply: n × n = n².

quiz.q: A loop does `i = i * 2` until i reaches n. Its complexity is…
quiz.why: i doubles each time, so it reaches n after about log₂ n steps.

quiz.q: n can be up to 10⁵. Which solution is safe?
quiz.why: 10⁵ × log(10⁵) ≈ 1.7 million steps — fine. n² = 10¹⁰ is far too slow.

topics.revision_note_md:
## Sorting — every method at a glance

| Sort | Time (avg / worst) | Space | Stable | Pick it when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bubble | n² / n² | 1 | ✅ | teaching; detect 'already sorted' |
| Selection | n² / n² | 1 | ❌ | writes are expensive |
| Insertion | n² / n² (n if sorted) | 1 | ✅ | small or nearly sorted |
| Shell | ~n^1.3 / n² | 1 | ❌ | simple in-place, no recursion |
| Merge | n log n / n log n | n | ✅ | stability, linked lists, external |
| Quick | n log n / n² | log n | ❌ | fastest general in-memory |
| Heap | n log n / n log n | 1 | ❌ | guarantee + O(1) space |
| Counting | n + k | n + k | ✅ | small integer range |
| Radix | d(n + b) | n + b | ✅ | fixed-length keys |
| Bucket | n + k / n² | n + k | ✅ | uniform real values |
| Cyclic | n | 1 | ❌ | values exactly 1..n |

- Comparison sorts can't beat **n log n**; counting/radix/bucket avoid comparisons.
- In JS always pass a comparator for numbers: `arr.sort((a, b) => a - b)`.

lesson.simple:
Sorting puts items in order. There are many ways to do it, and each one teaches a different idea:

- **Simple sorts** — bubble, selection, insertion (and shell, an upgraded insertion sort) — build intuition about loops, swaps and why O(n²) is slow.
- **Divide and conquer** — merge sort and quick sort — split the problem and get O(n log n).
- **Heap sort** — uses a data structure to guarantee O(n log n) with no extra memory.
- **Non-comparison sorts** — counting, radix, bucket and cyclic sort — use the values themselves to beat n log n when the data allows it.

Interviews test two things: **(1)** can you explain these methods and their trade-offs (stable? in place? worst case?), and **(2)** do you notice when *sorting first* makes a hard problem easy. Each method below has a visualiser — press **Play**, step through it, or type your own numbers — and a video clip that plays only the part about that method.
lesson.analogy: Merge sort is two teachers each sorting half the exam papers, then merging their piles by always picking the lower roll number from the top of the two piles.

concepts.title: The words used to describe sorts
concepts.body:
Every sorting algorithm is judged on the same few properties. Learn these words first — interview questions are usually *"which sort is stable / in place / best for X?"*

- **Time complexity** in the best, average and worst case.
- **Space** — extra memory beyond the input. **In place** means O(1) extra (or O(log n) for recursion).
- **Stable** — equal items keep their original order. Matters when you sort records by one field after another.
- **Adaptive** — runs faster when the input is already nearly sorted (insertion sort, bubble sort with early stop, Timsort).
- **Comparison vs non-comparison** — most sorts only compare pairs (`a < b`). Counting, radix and bucket sort instead use the *values themselves* as positions.

**The lower bound:** any sort that only compares pairs needs **Ω(n log n)** comparisons in the worst case. There are n! possible orderings, each comparison has two outcomes, so you need at least log₂(n!) ≈ n log n of them to tell all orderings apart. Counting, radix and bucket sort beat this only because they don't rely on comparisons — and only on suitable data.

| Algorithm | Best | Average | Worst | Extra space | Stable | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bubble | O(n) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | ✅ | early stop when no swaps |
| Selection | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | ❌ | fewest swaps (≤ n − 1) |
| Insertion | O(n) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | ✅ | best for small / nearly sorted |
| Shell | O(n log n) | ~O(n^1.3) | O(n²) | O(1) | ❌ | depends on gap sequence |
| Merge | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n) | ✅ | great for linked lists |
| Quick | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n²) | O(log n) | ❌ | fastest in practice |
| Heap | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(1) | ❌ | guaranteed, in place |
| Counting | O(n + k) | O(n + k) | O(n + k) | O(n + k) | ✅ | k = value range |
| Radix | O(d·(n + b)) | O(d·(n + b)) | O(d·(n + b)) | O(n + b) | ✅ | d digits, base b |
| Bucket | O(n + k) | O(n + k) | O(n²) | O(n + k) | ✅* | needs uniform data |
| Cyclic | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) | ❌ | only for values 1..n |

\* stable if each bucket uses a stable sort.

concepts.title: Bubble sort
concepts.body:
**Idea:** walk through the array comparing **neighbours** and swap them if they're in the wrong order. After the first pass, the largest value has "bubbled" to the end. Repeat on the unsorted part.

**Steps**
1. For pass = 0, 1, 2, …: compare `a[j]` and `a[j + 1]` for every j in the unsorted part; swap if `a[j] > a[j + 1]`.
2. After each pass the last unsorted position is final, so the next pass can stop one earlier.
3. If a whole pass makes **no swaps**, the array is sorted — stop early.

```python
def bubble_sort(a):
    n = len(a)
    for p in range(n - 1):
        swapped = False
        for j in range(n - 1 - p):
            if a[j] > a[j + 1]:
                a[j], a[j + 1] = a[j + 1], a[j]
                swapped = True
        if not swapped:          # already sorted → O(n) best case
            break
    return a
```

**Complexity:** O(n²) average and worst; **O(n) best** (already sorted, thanks to the early stop). O(1) space. **Stable**, because it only swaps when strictly greater.

**Use it when:** almost never in production. It's asked to check you understand loops, swaps and the early-exit optimisation. Its one real strength is detecting "already sorted" in a single pass.

concepts.title: Selection sort
concepts.body:
**Idea:** repeatedly **select the smallest** remaining value and put it at the front of the unsorted part.

**Steps**
1. For i = 0 … n − 2: find the index of the minimum in `a[i:]`.
2. Swap it into position i. Position i is now final.

```python
def selection_sort(a):
    n = len(a)
    for i in range(n - 1):
        m = i
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if a[j] < a[m]:
                m = j
        a[i], a[m] = a[m], a[i]
    return a
```

**Complexity:** always O(n²) comparisons — even on sorted input, because it must scan the rest to be sure it found the minimum. O(1) space. **Not stable**: the long-distance swap can jump an item over an equal one (sort `[2a, 2b, 1]` → `[1, 2b, 2a]`).

**Use it when:** writes are expensive (e.g. flash memory) — it does **at most n − 1 swaps**, fewer than any other simple sort. Interviews ask it mainly to contrast with insertion sort.

concepts.title: Insertion sort
concepts.body:
**Idea:** grow a sorted section on the left. Take the next item and **slide it left** until it's in the right spot — exactly how you sort playing cards in your hand.

**Steps**
1. For i = 1 … n − 1: `key = a[i]`.
2. Shift every item in the sorted part that's bigger than key one step right.
3. Drop key into the gap.

```python
def insertion_sort(a):
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        key, j = a[i], i - 1
        while j >= 0 and a[j] > key:
            a[j + 1] = a[j]        # shift right
            j -= 1
        a[j + 1] = key
    return a
```

**Complexity:** O(n²) average and worst (reversed input), but **O(n) on sorted input**, and in general O(n + inversions) — so it's very fast on **nearly sorted** data. O(1) space, **stable**, and it can sort data **as it arrives** (online).

**Use it when:** the array is small (≲ 20–50 items) or nearly sorted. That's why Timsort (Python, Java) and introsort (C++) switch to insertion sort for small pieces.

concepts.title: Shell sort
concepts.body:
**Idea:** insertion sort is slow because items move **one step at a time**. Shell sort first sorts items that are far apart (a big **gap**), so small values jump close to the front quickly, then repeats with smaller gaps. The last pass, gap 1, is a plain insertion sort — but on nearly sorted data, so it's fast.

```python
def shell_sort(a):
    gap = len(a) // 2
    while gap > 0:
        for i in range(gap, len(a)):        # insertion sort with stride = gap
            key, j = a[i], i
            while j >= gap and a[j - gap] > key:
                a[j] = a[j - gap]
                j -= gap
            a[j] = key
        gap //= 2
    return a
```

**Complexity:** depends on the gap sequence. Halving gaps (n/2, n/4, … 1) is O(n²) worst case; better sequences (Knuth's 1, 4, 13, 40…, or Ciura's) are around O(n^1.3) in practice. O(1) space, **not stable**.

**Use it when:** you need an in-place sort with little code and no recursion (embedded systems). In interviews it's a "do you know beyond the basics?" question — explain the gap idea and why it helps insertion sort.

concepts.title: Merge sort
concepts.body:
**Idea — divide and conquer:**
1. **Divide** the array into two halves.
2. **Sort** each half recursively (one item is already sorted).
3. **Merge** the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front item.

```python
def merge_sort(a):
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return a
    mid = len(a) // 2
    left, right = merge_sort(a[:mid]), merge_sort(a[mid:])
    out, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:        # <= keeps it stable
            out.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else:
            out.append(right[j]); j += 1
    return out + left[i:] + right[j:]
```

**Why O(n log n) always:** halving creates log₂ n levels; at each level the merges together touch every item once. n per level × log n levels — in the best, average **and** worst case.

**Trade-offs:** O(n) extra memory for merging; **stable**. Not adaptive in its basic form (Timsort is the adaptive descendant).

**Use it when:** you need a guaranteed O(n log n) or stability; for **linked lists** (merging needs no random access and no extra array); for **external sorting** of data bigger than memory. Bonus: counting **inversions** during the merge is a classic follow-up.

concepts.title: Quick sort
concepts.body:
**Idea:** pick a **pivot**, **partition** the array so smaller items are on its left and larger on its right — the pivot is now in its final place — then sort both sides the same way.

```python
def quick_sort(a, lo=0, hi=None):
    if hi is None:
        hi = len(a) - 1
    if lo >= hi:
        return a
    pivot, i = a[hi], lo                 # Lomuto partition, pivot = last item
    for j in range(lo, hi):
        if a[j] < pivot:
            a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
            i += 1
    a[i], a[hi] = a[hi], a[i]            # pivot to its final index
    quick_sort(a, lo, i - 1)
    quick_sort(a, i + 1, hi)
    return a
```

**Complexity:** if pivots split roughly in half, depth is log n → **O(n log n)**. If the pivot is always the smallest or largest (last-element pivot on sorted input), each call removes one item → **O(n²)**. Fixes: a **random pivot** or **median-of-three**; for many duplicates, **3-way partitioning** (Dutch national flag). Space O(log n) for recursion on average. **Not stable**.

**Use it when:** you want the fastest general in-memory sort — it scans memory sequentially and sorts in place, which is why it's the base of most library sorts (with safeguards). **Quickselect** uses the same partition to find the k-th smallest in O(n) on average.

concepts.title: Heap sort
concepts.body:
**Idea:** use a **max-heap** (every parent ≥ its children, stored in the array itself) to repeatedly pull out the largest item.

**Steps**
1. **Build a max-heap** in place: sift down every non-leaf node from the last one to the root — O(n).
2. Swap the root (the max) with the last item of the heap; the end of the array is now sorted.
3. Shrink the heap by one and **sift the new root down** to restore the heap. Repeat.

```python
def heap_sort(a):
    def sift_down(root, end):              # end is inclusive
        while 2 * root + 1 <= end:
            child = 2 * root + 1
            if child + 1 <= end and a[child] < a[child + 1]:
                child += 1                 # bigger child
            if a[root] >= a[child]:
                return
            a[root], a[child] = a[child], a[root]
            root = child
    n = len(a)
    for start in range(n // 2 - 1, -1, -1):
        sift_down(start, n - 1)
    for end in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
        a[0], a[end] = a[end], a[0]
        sift_down(0, end - 1)
    return a
```

**Complexity:** **O(n log n) in every case** and **O(1) extra space** — the only common sort with both guarantees. **Not stable**, and slower than quick sort in practice because it jumps around memory.

**Use it when:** you need a worst-case guarantee without extra memory (introsort falls back to heap sort when quick sort's recursion gets too deep). The heap itself is the bigger interview topic — see the Heaps lesson.

concepts.title: Counting sort
concepts.body:
**Idea:** if values are small integers in a known range 0..k, don't compare at all — **count** how many times each value appears, then write the values back in order.

```python
def counting_sort(a):
    if not a:
        return a
    k = max(a)
    count = [0] * (k + 1)
    for v in a:
        count[v] += 1
    # stable version: prefix sums tell each value where its block ends
    for v in range(1, k + 1):
        count[v] += count[v - 1]
    out = [0] * len(a)
    for v in reversed(a):                 # reversed keeps equal items in order
        count[v] -= 1
        out[count[v]] = v
    return out
```

The visualiser shows the simple version (write each value count[v] times). The **prefix-sum version** above matters when you sort **records by a key**: it places each record directly in its final slot and keeps equal keys in their original order — that stability is what makes radix sort work.

**Complexity:** **O(n + k)** time and space. Great when k is about the size of n or smaller (ages, grades, characters); terrible when k is huge (sorting a few 32-bit numbers would need billions of counters).

**Interview uses:** Sort Colors (k = 3), sorting characters by frequency, H-Index, "sort by age", and as the inner step of radix sort.

concepts.title: Radix sort
concepts.body:
**Idea:** sort numbers **digit by digit**. LSD (least significant digit first) radix sort does one **stable** pass per digit: first by the ones digit, then the tens, then the hundreds… Because each pass is stable, the order from earlier (less important) digits survives among numbers that tie on the current digit.

```python
def radix_sort(a):                        # non-negative integers
    if not a:
        return a
    exp = 1
    while max(a) // exp > 0:
        buckets = [[] for _ in range(10)]
        for v in a:
            buckets[(v // exp) % 10].append(v)   # stable: keeps arrival order
        a = [v for b in buckets for v in b]
        exp *= 10
    return a
```

**Complexity:** **O(d · (n + b))** for d digits in base b. For 32-bit integers with base 256 that's 4 passes over the data — linear in practice. Extra space O(n + b).

**Watch out:** negative numbers need an offset or separate handling; strings sort with MSD (most significant first) radix. Radix sort shines for many fixed-length keys: integers, dates, IP addresses, fixed-length strings.

**Interview use:** *Maximum Gap* (sort in linear time, then scan) and as the answer to "can you sort faster than n log n?" — yes, when keys have limited digits.

concepts.title: Bucket sort
concepts.body:
**Idea:** spread the values into **buckets by range** (0–19, 20–39, …), sort each small bucket (usually with insertion sort), then concatenate the buckets in order.

```python
def bucket_sort(a, buckets=5):
    if not a:
        return a
    lo, hi = min(a), max(a)
    width = (hi - lo) / buckets or 1
    groups = [[] for _ in range(buckets)]
    for v in a:
        i = min(buckets - 1, int((v - lo) / width))
        groups[i].append(v)
    return [v for g in groups for v in sorted(g)]
```

**Complexity:** if values are **spread evenly**, each bucket holds about n/k items and the total is **O(n + k)**. If they all land in one bucket, you're back to that bucket's sort — **O(n²)** with insertion sort. Space O(n + k).

**Use it when:** values are real numbers spread roughly uniformly over a known range (e.g. floats in [0, 1)), or for "top-k by frequency" where the bucket index is the frequency (*Top K Frequent Elements* in O(n)). The **pigeonhole** idea behind it also solves *Maximum Gap*: with n numbers and n − 1 buckets, the biggest gap must be between buckets, not inside one.

concepts.title: Cyclic sort (the 1..n pattern)
concepts.body:
**Idea:** when the array contains the numbers **1 to n** (maybe with some missing or duplicated), every value v has a known home: **index v − 1**. Walk through the array and keep swapping the current value into its home until the current index holds the right value.

```python
def cyclic_sort(a):                       # values 1..n
    i = 0
    while i < len(a):
        home = a[i] - 1
        if a[i] != a[home]:
            a[i], a[home] = a[home], a[i]   # put a[i] where it belongs
        else:
            i += 1                           # already home (or a duplicate)
    return a
```

**Complexity:** **O(n) time, O(1) space.** Each swap puts at least one value in its final home, so there are at most n swaps in total, even though there's a while loop.

**Why it's an interview favourite:** after cyclic sort, any index i where `a[i] != i + 1` tells you something:
- *Missing Number*, *Find All Numbers Disappeared* — the missing values are the indices whose value is wrong.
- *Find the Duplicate*, *Find All Duplicates*, *Set Mismatch* — the wrong values are the duplicates.
- *First Missing Positive* — ignore values outside 1..n, cyclic-sort the rest, return the first index that's wrong.

All in O(n) time and O(1) space, which is exactly what these questions demand.

concepts.title: Built-in sorts, stability and comparators
concepts.body:
In real code and most interviews you'll call the language's sort. Know what it does:

| Language | Algorithm | Stable | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Python `sorted`, `list.sort` | **Timsort** (merge + insertion, finds existing runs) | ✅ | O(n) on sorted data, O(n log n) worst |
| JavaScript `Array.prototype.sort` | Timsort in V8 | ✅ (required since ES2019) | compares as **strings** without a comparator |
| Java `Arrays.sort` | dual-pivot quick sort for primitives, Timsort for objects | objects ✅ | |
| C++ `std::sort` / `std::stable_sort` | introsort (quick + heap + insertion) / merge | ❌ / ✅ | |

**Multi-key sorting:**
```python
people.sort(key=lambda p: (p.dept, -p.salary, p.name))   # dept ↑, salary ↓, name ↑
```
```javascript
people.sort((a, b) => a.dept.localeCompare(b.dept) || b.salary - a.salary || a.name.localeCompare(b.name));
```
A JS comparator returns negative if `a` goes first, positive if `b` goes first, 0 if equal. Without one, `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]`.

**Custom orders** — *Largest Number*: sort strings with the comparator "a before b if a + b > b + a" (`functools.cmp_to_key` in Python).

concepts.title: When sorting is the real trick
concepts.body:
Many problems become easy after sorting, and O(n log n) is usually acceptable:

- **Pairs and triplets with a target** (Two Sum II, 3Sum) → sort, then two pointers.
- **Intervals** (merge intervals, meeting rooms) → sort by start (or by end for greedy selection).
- **Duplicates and grouping** → equal items become neighbours; anagrams group by their sorted letters.
- **"Closest" / "minimum difference"** → after sorting, the best pair is always adjacent.
- **Greedy assignment** (cookies to children, boats) → sort both sides and match.
- **Values in 1..n** → cyclic sort, O(n) and O(1) space.
- **Small value range** → counting sort, O(n + k).

How to choose in an interview:
1. Is the data small or nearly sorted? → insertion sort / the built-in sort.
2. Do I need stability or a linked list? → merge sort.
3. Do I need O(1) extra space with a guarantee? → heap sort.
4. Are the values small integers, fixed-length keys or 1..n? → counting / radix / cyclic sort.
5. Otherwise → the built-in sort, and say it's Timsort / introsort under the hood.

dry_run.takeaway: Merging two sorted lists is linear. Splitting gives log n levels, each merging n items → O(n log n).

template.python:
def merge_sort(arr):
    if len(arr) <= 1:
        return arr
    mid = len(arr) // 2
    left, right = merge_sort(arr[:mid]), merge_sort(arr[mid:])
    merged, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:      # <= keeps it stable
            merged.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else:
            merged.append(right[j]); j += 1
    merged.extend(left[i:])
    merged.extend(right[j:])
    return merged

topics.revision_note_md:
## Arrays

- Access by index is O(1); inserting/deleting in the middle is O(n).
- Most array tricks: **one pass with a variable** (running max/min), **frequency map**, **in-place swaps**, **prefix sums**.
- Ask: is it sorted? can values be negative? are there duplicates?

lesson.simple:
An array is a row of boxes numbered 0, 1, 2… Most array questions are solved by **walking through once** while remembering something useful — the smallest value so far, a count, or a position to write to.

The beginner jump is from *"try every pair"* (O(n²)) to *"walk once and remember the right thing"* (O(n)).
lesson.analogy: Tracking the cheapest day to buy gold: you scroll through past prices once, remembering the lowest price so far, and at each day ask "if I sold today, how much would I gain?"

concepts.title: How arrays work in memory
concepts.body:
An array stores items **side by side in memory**. Because every slot has the same size, the address of item i is `start + i × size`, so reading or writing `a[i]` is **O(1)**.

The cost shows up when you change the length in the middle:
- **Insert or delete at index i** → every item after i shifts by one: **O(n)**.
- **Append at the end** → O(1) amortised. When a dynamic array (Python list, JS array) is full, it allocates a bigger block (about 1.5–2×) and copies everything; that rare O(n) copy averages out to O(1) per append.
- **Pop from the end** → O(1). **Pop from the front** (`list.pop(0)`, `shift()`) → O(n). Use `collections.deque` for queues.

This is why many array tricks work *from the end* or use a separate **write pointer** instead of deleting items.

concepts.title: The running-state pattern (one pass, remember the right thing)
concepts.body:
Most O(n) array solutions walk once and keep a small piece of state:

| Question | State to keep |
|---|---|
| Best profit buying then selling | minimum price so far |
| Maximum subarray sum (Kadane) | best sum ending at the current index |
| Majority element | candidate + counter (Boyer–Moore) |
| Longest streak of 1s | current streak, best streak |

**Kadane's algorithm** is the most important example. At each index, the best subarray *ending here* either extends the previous one or starts fresh:

```python
best = cur = nums[0]
for x in nums[1:]:
    cur = max(x, cur + x)     # extend or restart
    best = max(best, cur)
```

The habit to build: ask *"if I knew the answer for everything up to i − 1, what's the smallest thing I'd need to remember to get the answer at i?"*

concepts.title: Prefix sums: answering range questions instantly
concepts.body:
A **prefix sum** array stores running totals: `prefix[i]` = sum of the first i items. Then the sum of any range `[l, r]` is `prefix[r + 1] − prefix[l]` — O(1) after O(n) setup.

The real power comes from combining prefix sums with a **hash map**. *"Count subarrays that sum to k"*: a subarray `(j, i]` sums to k exactly when `prefix[i] − prefix[j] = k`, i.e. when you've previously seen the prefix value `prefix[i] − k`.

```python
from collections import defaultdict
def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    seen, total, count = defaultdict(int), 0, 0
    seen[0] = 1                      # empty prefix
    for x in nums:
        total += x
        count += seen[total - k]
        seen[total] += 1
    return count
```

This works with **negative numbers**, where sliding window fails. Variants: product of array except self (prefix and suffix products), 2D prefix sums for matrix region queries.

concepts.title: In-place techniques: write pointers, swaps and reversals
concepts.body:
When the problem says *"in place"* or *"O(1) extra space"*, reach for these:

- **Write pointer** — a `write` index marks where the next kept item goes; a `read` index scans everything. Used for removing duplicates, removing a value, moving zeroes. Keeps order and runs in O(n).
- **Swaps with boundaries** — Dutch national flag (Sort Colors) keeps `low`, `mid`, `high` pointers and swaps items into three regions in one pass.
- **Reversal tricks** — rotating right by k = reverse all, reverse the first k, reverse the rest. Each reversal is O(n) with O(1) space.
- **Using the array as its own hash map** — when values are in the range 1..n, mark "seen" by negating `a[value − 1]` (find duplicates, first missing positive).

Always say the trade-off: in-place saves memory but destroys the input, so ask if that's allowed.

concepts.title: Matrices: indices, boundaries and directions
concepts.body:
A matrix is an array of arrays; `grid[r][c]` is row r, column c. Most matrix problems are about **walking the indices correctly**:

- **Directions list** — `[(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]` for right, down, left, up. Bounds check: `0 <= r < rows and 0 <= c < cols`.
- **Spiral order** — keep four boundaries (`top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`); walk one edge, then shrink that boundary. Stop when they cross.
- **Rotate 90° clockwise in place** — transpose (swap `m[i][j]` with `m[j][i]`), then reverse each row.
- **Set Matrix Zeroes in O(1) space** — use the first row and first column as marker storage, with one extra flag for the first column itself.

Flattening helps too: cell `(r, c)` ↔ index `r × cols + c`. That's how you binary search a sorted matrix as if it were one array.

topics.description: Eliminate half of search space in every step on sorted or monotonic search spaces in O(log n) time.
topics.revision_note_md:
## Pattern 10 — Binary Search

**Core idea:** on a sorted array (or any monotonic space), eliminate half the search space every step by comparing the middle element to the target. O(log n) instead of O(n).

**Decision trigger:** sorted array + "find target / find first/last position / find minimum." Also applies to problems where the answer itself is a number in a range, and you can check "is X a valid answer?" in O(n) — that check is your predicate, binary search finds the boundary.

**The two shapes:**
- **Search for a value** — classic binary search on a sorted array.
- **Binary search on the answer** — the search space is a range of possible answers (e.g., minimum capacity, minimum days), and you binary search for the smallest valid one.

items.title: Binary Search
hints: mid = (left + right) // 2.
If nums[mid] == target, return mid; if nums[mid] < target, left = mid + 1.

items.python:
def search(nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    l, r = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while l <= r:
        mid = (l + r) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target: return mid
        elif nums[mid] < target: l = mid + 1
        else: r = mid - 1
    return -1

lesson.simple:
Binary search finds something in a **sorted** list by checking the middle and throwing away the half that can't contain the answer. Each step halves the search space, so even a million items take only ~20 steps.

The bigger idea: binary search works on **any yes/no question that flips once** — "can Koko finish eating at speed k?" is *no, no, no, yes, yes*. Find the first yes.
lesson.analogy: Guess-the-number game: "Is it more than 50?" "Yes." "More than 75?" "No." You never guess one by one.

concepts.title: The invariant: what lo and hi always mean
concepts.body:
Binary search works on anything **sorted** or, more generally, anything where a yes/no question flips **once** from no to yes (or yes to no). Each step looks at the middle and throws away the half that can't contain the answer, so it takes **O(log n)** steps — about 20 steps for a million items.

Most bugs come from not deciding what `lo` and `hi` *mean*. Pick one style and keep it:

**Closed range `[lo, hi]`** — the answer, if it exists, is between lo and hi inclusive.
```python
lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
while lo <= hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if a[mid] == target: return mid
    if a[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
    else: hi = mid - 1
return -1
```

**Half-open "first true"** — find the first index where `ok(i)` is True; `hi` can be one past the end.
```python
lo, hi = 0, len(a)
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if ok(mid): hi = mid
    else: lo = mid + 1
return lo
```

concepts.title: Lower bound, upper bound and counting occurrences
concepts.body:
Two "first true" searches answer most questions about duplicates:

- **lower_bound(x)** — first index with `a[i] >= x`. This is where x would be inserted to keep order (Python's `bisect_left`).
- **upper_bound(x)** — first index with `a[i] > x` (`bisect_right`).

From them:
- **First occurrence** of x = lower_bound(x), if `a[that] == x`.
- **Last occurrence** = upper_bound(x) − 1.
- **Count of x** = upper_bound(x) − lower_bound(x).
- **Floor** (largest ≤ x) = upper_bound(x) − 1; **ceil** (smallest ≥ x) = lower_bound(x).

Python gives you these via `import bisect`; in an interview, write the loop once and say you'd use the library in production.

concepts.title: Rotated arrays: one half is always sorted
concepts.body:
A sorted array rotated at an unknown point, e.g. `[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]`, isn't sorted overall — but if you split it at any `mid`, **at least one half is sorted**.

The decision at each step:
1. If `a[lo] <= a[mid]`, the **left half is sorted**. If the target lies in `[a[lo], a[mid])`, search left; otherwise search right.
2. Else the **right half is sorted**. If the target lies in `(a[mid], a[hi]]`, search right; otherwise search left.

To find the **minimum** (the rotation point): compare `a[mid]` with `a[hi]`. If `a[mid] > a[hi]`, the minimum is to the right of mid; otherwise it's at mid or to the left (`hi = mid`).

With **duplicates** (e.g. `[1, 1, 1, 0, 1]`) you sometimes can't tell which half is sorted; shrink with `hi -= 1` and accept O(n) worst case — mention this edge case.

concepts.title: Binary search on the answer
concepts.body:
The most powerful form doesn't search an array at all. You **guess the answer** and check if it's feasible, when feasibility is **monotonic**: if speed k works, any faster speed also works.

Recipe:
1. Define the answer's range: smallest possible to largest possible.
2. Write `feasible(x)` — usually a greedy O(n) check.
3. Binary search for the **smallest x where feasible(x) is True** (or the largest, depending on the problem).

**Koko eating bananas:** range of speeds `[1, max(piles)]`; `feasible(k)` = total hours `sum(ceil(p / k))` ≤ h. Total cost: O(n log max).

The same shape solves *"minimum capacity to ship packages in D days"*, *"split array to minimise the largest sum"*, *"minimum days to make m bouquets"* and *"aggressive cows"*. The signal in the wording: **"minimise the maximum"** or **"maximise the minimum"**.

concepts.title: Off-by-one checklist
concepts.body:
Before you say you're done, check:

- **Overflow-safe middle** — in Java/C++ use `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`. Python ints don't overflow, but say it.
- **Loop condition matches the range style** — `lo <= hi` for closed, `lo < hi` for half-open.
- **Progress is guaranteed** — with `lo < hi` and `mid = (lo + hi) // 2`, setting `lo = mid` can loop forever when `hi = lo + 1`. Use `lo = mid + 1`, or round mid up (`(lo + hi + 1) // 2`) when you need `lo = mid`.
- **Empty input and single element.**
- **Target smaller than everything / larger than everything** — trace both quickly.

topics.description: Character counting, palindromes, anagrams and string building — the basics before string patterns.
topics.revision_note_md:
## Strings

- Strings are arrays of characters; in Python and JS they are **immutable** — building with `+=` in a loop can be O(n²). Use a list and `join`.
- Toolkit: **frequency count** (array of 26 or a map), **two pointers** (palindromes, reversing), **sliding window** (substrings).

lesson.simple:
Most string questions are really **counting** questions or **two-ends** questions.

- *Are these two words anagrams?* → count each letter in both and compare.
- *Is it a palindrome?* → compare the first and last character, move inward.
- *Longest substring with some rule?* → sliding window (next lesson).
lesson.analogy: Checking anagrams is like checking two bags of Scrabble tiles: you don't care about order, only whether both bags have the same count of each letter.

concepts.title: Strings are immutable: build them the right way
concepts.body:
In Python and JavaScript you can't change a character inside a string; every "change" creates a **new string**. That has a cost:

```python
s = ""
for ch in chars:
    s += ch          # may copy the whole string each time → O(n²) worst case
```

Build a **list of pieces and join once** at the end — O(n):
```python
parts = []
for ch in chars:
    parts.append(ch)
s = "".join(parts)
```
In JS, push into an array and `join('')`. When you need to modify characters in place (reverse words, swap), convert to a list first: `arr = list(s)`.

Also remember slicing `s[i:j]` copies j − i characters — O(k), not O(1). Comparing two strings is O(length) too.

concepts.title: Character counting: the 26-slot array vs a hash map
concepts.body:
Many string problems are really **counting problems**: anagrams, "can I build this note from that magazine?", first unique character, minimum window.

- If the input is **lowercase letters only**, use a fixed array: `count[ord(ch) - ord('a')] += 1`. It's fast and its size is O(1) (26 slots).
- For **any characters** (Unicode, mixed case, digits), use a dict / `Counter` / `Map`.

Comparing two counts is O(26) for the array version. A neat trick for anagrams: **increment for s and decrement for t in the same loop**, then check every slot is zero.

**Grouping anagrams:** use a key that's identical for all anagrams — either the sorted word (`"".join(sorted(w))`, O(k log k)) or a tuple of the 26 counts (O(k)).

concepts.title: Parsing strings safely
concepts.body:
Questions like *String to Integer (atoi)*, *Decode String* and *Valid Number* test careful step-by-step parsing. A structure that keeps you safe:

1. Use an **index `i`** and advance it explicitly instead of splitting and slicing everywhere.
2. Handle phases in order — e.g. atoi: skip spaces → optional sign → digits → stop at the first non-digit.
3. Build numbers digit by digit: `value = value * 10 + int(ch)`.
4. Check limits **before** overflowing (32-bit range: −2³¹ to 2³¹ − 1).
5. Write down the edge cases first: empty string, only spaces, sign with no digits, leading zeros, huge numbers.

Nested structures (`"3[a2[c]]"`) use a **stack**: push the current string and repeat count when you see `[`, pop and combine at `]`.

topics.name: Two Pointers
topics.description: Use two indices moving through an array, string, or linked list based on a condition — instead of nested loops. Turns O(n²) into O(n).
topics.revision_note_md:
## Pattern 1 — Two Pointer

**Core idea:** use two indices moving through an array, string, or linked list based on a condition — instead of nested loops. Turns O(n²) into O(n).

**Precondition:** array is sorted (or sortable), or the problem has a structural property (palindrome, partitioning, linked list) that lets you reason about both ends or both speeds at once.

**Decision trigger:** sorted array + pair/triplet/quadruplet condition, in-place compaction, palindrome check, or linked list cycle/middle.

**Three flavors:**
- **Opposite direction** → `left=0`, `right=n-1`, converge toward each other. Used when sorted order makes the two extremes meaningful.
- **Same direction (slow/fast)** → both start near 0, fast scans forward, slow marks the "finalized" boundary. Used for in-place compaction.
- **Fast-slow on linked lists** → fast moves 2 nodes per step, slow moves 1. Used for cycle detection and finding the middle node.

items.title: Two Sum II – Input Array Is Sorted
hints: Place left pointer at index 0 and right pointer at index n-1.
If sum < target, increment left; if sum > target, decrement right.
items.explanation: Since array is sorted, sum increases by moving left rightward and decreases by moving right leftward.

items.title: Valid Palindrome
hints: Filter or skip non-alphanumeric characters.
Compare lowercase characters from both ends moving inward.
items.explanation: Use two pointers starting at opposite ends. Skip non-alphanumeric chars and verify character equality.
items.python:
def isPalindrome(s: str) -> bool:
    l, r = 0, len(s) - 1
    while l < r:
        while l < r and not s[l].isalnum(): l += 1
        while l < r and not s[r].isalnum(): r -= 1
        if s[l].lower() != s[r].lower(): return False
        l += 1; r -= 1
    return True

Skip duplicate elements to ensure unique triplets.

items.python:
def threeSum(nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
    nums.sort()
    res = []
    for i in range(len(nums) - 2):
        if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1]: continue
        l, r = i + 1, len(nums) - 1
        while l < r:
            s = nums[i] + nums[l] + nums[r]
            if s == 0:
                res.append([nums[i], nums[l], nums[r]])
                while l < r and nums[l] == nums[l+1]: l += 1
                while l < r and nums[r] == nums[r-1]: r -= 1
                l += 1; r -= 1
            elif s < 0: l += 1
            else: r -= 1
    return res

hints: Sort array and fix first element.

hints: Width decreases as pointers move inward.
To get larger area, move the pointer pointing to shorter line.
items.explanation: Area is min(height[l], height[r]) * (r - l). Move whichever pointer has smaller height.
items.python:
def maxArea(height: list[int]) -> int:
    l, r = 0, len(height) - 1
    max_water = 0
    while l < r:
        water = min(height[l], height[r]) * (r - l)
        max_water = max(max_water, water)
        if height[l] < height[r]: l += 1
        else: r -= 1
    return max_water

Fast moves 2 steps, slow moves 1 step. If cycle exists, fast meets slow.
items.explanation: Floyd's Cycle Finding Algorithm. Fast pointer advances 2 nodes, slow pointer 1 node.
items.python:
def hasCycle(head) -> bool:
    slow, fast = head, head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow == fast: return True
    return False

hints: Fast moves 2 steps, slow moves 1 step.
When fast reaches end, slow is at the middle.
items.explanation: Fast moves twice as fast as slow. When fast reaches null or fast.next is null, slow is at the middle node.

items.title: Subarray Product Less Than K
hints: Use sliding window / two pointers (right expands, left shrinks).
Count of valid subarrays ending at right is (right - left + 1).
items.explanation: Maintain product of sliding window [left, right]. Shrink left while product >= k. Add (right - left + 1) to count.

items.title: Trapping Rain Water
hints: Maintain left_max and right_max.
Water at position is bounded by min(left_max, right_max) - height.
items.explanation: Two pointers from ends. Process side with smaller max height, maintaining left_max and right_max.
items.python:
def trap(height: list[int]) -> int:
    l, r = 0, len(height) - 1
    left_max, right_max = 0, 0
    water = 0
    while l < r:
        if height[l] < height[r]:
            if height[l] >= left_max: left_max = height[l]
            else: water += left_max - height[l]
            l += 1
        else:
            if height[r] >= right_max: right_max = height[r]
            else: water += right_max - height[r]
            r -= 1
    return water

items.title: 4Sum

Use two nested loops for first two numbers, two pointers for remaining two numbers.
items.explanation: Sort array. Fix i and j, use two pointers l and r. Skip duplicates at every level to get unique quadruplets.
items.python:
def fourSum(nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[list[int]]:
    nums.sort()
    n = len(nums)
    res = []
    for i in range(n - 3):
        if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1]: continue
        for j in range(i + 1, n - 2):
            if j > i + 1 and nums[j] == nums[j-1]: continue
            l, r = j + 1, n - 1
            while l < r:
                s = nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[l] + nums[r]
                if s == target:
                    res.append([nums[i], nums[j], nums[l], nums[r]])
                    while l < r and nums[l] == nums[l+1]: l += 1
                    while l < r and nums[r] == nums[r-1]: r -= 1
                    l += 1; r -= 1
                elif s < target: l += 1
                else: r -= 1
    return res

items.title: Backspace String Compare
hints: Iterate backward from the end of both strings.
Track backspace counts to skip characters.
items.explanation: Two pointers traversing right-to-left. Accumulate backspaces '#' to skip valid characters.
items.python:
def backspaceCompare(s: str, t: str) -> bool:
    def get_valid_idx(string, idx):
        skip = 0
        while idx >= 0:
            if string[idx] == '#': skip += 1; idx -= 1
            elif skip > 0: skip -= 1; idx -= 1
            else: break
        return idx
    i, j = len(s) - 1, len(t) - 1
    while i >= 0 or j >= 0:
        i = get_valid_idx(s, i)
        j = get_valid_idx(t, j)
        if i >= 0 and j >= 0 and s[i] != t[j]: return False
        if (i >= 0) != (j >= 0): return False
        i -= 1; j -= 1
    return True

items.title: Boats to Save People
hints: Sort weights array.
Pair heaviest person with lightest person if sum <= limit.
items.explanation: Greedy approach using two pointers on sorted array. Always pair heaviest with lightest if possible.

items.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
hints: Use sliding window (left and right pointers).
Expand right to reach target sum, then shrink left to find minimum length.
items.explanation: Sliding window technique. Expand right pointer accumulating sum; while sum >= target, record min length and increment left.
items.python:
def minSubArrayLen(target: int, nums: list[int]) -> int:
    l = 0
    current_sum = 0
    min_len = float('inf')
    for r in range(len(nums)):
        current_sum += nums[r]
        while current_sum >= target:
            min_len = min(min_len, r - l + 1)
            current_sum -= nums[l]
            l += 1
    return min_len if min_len != float('inf') else 0

items.title: Shortest Unsorted Continuous Subarray
hints: Find maximum from left and minimum from right.
Identify boundary where values violate sorted order.
items.explanation: Traverse left to right tracking max value to find right boundary. Traverse right to left tracking min value to find left boundary.
items.python:
def findUnsortedSubarray(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(nums)
    max_val, min_val = float('-inf'), float('inf')
    l, r = -1, -1
    for i in range(n):
        max_val = max(max_val, nums[i])
        if nums[i] < max_val: r = i
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        min_val = min(min_val, nums[i])
        if nums[i] > min_val: l = i
    return r - l + 1 if r != -1 else 0

hints: Fill nums1 from back to front.
Use pointers at m-1, n-1, and write pointer at m+n-1.

items.title: Longest Duplicate Substring
hints: Use Binary Search on length of duplicate substring.
Use Rabin-Karp (rolling hash) to check for duplicate of length L in O(N).
items.explanation: Binary search on length from 1 to N-1. Check duplicate existence using Rabin-Karp algorithm.
items.python:
def longestDuplicateSubstring(s: str) -> str:
    import functools
    n = len(s)
    nums = [ord(c) - ord('a') for c in s]
    mod = 2**63 - 1
    def search(length):
        h = 0
        for i in range(length): h = (h * 26 + nums[i]) % mod
        seen = {h}
        aL = pow(26, length, mod)
        for start in range(1, n - length + 1):
            h = (h * 26 - nums[start - 1] * aL + nums[start + length - 1]) % mod
            if h in seen: return start
            seen.add(h)
        return -1
    l, r = 1, n - 1
    start_idx = -1
    max_len = 0
    while l <= r:
        mid = (l + r) // 2
        idx = search(mid)
        if idx != -1:
            start_idx = idx
            max_len = mid
            l = mid + 1
        else: r = mid - 1
    return s[start_idx:start_idx + max_len] if start_idx != -1 else ''

lesson.simple:
Two pointers means using **two indices** that move through the data instead of checking every pair. It turns many O(n²) brute forces into O(n).

Two common styles:
- **Opposite ends** (sorted array): `left` at the start, `right` at the end. If the sum is too small move `left` right; too big move `right` left.
- **Same direction**: a `slow` pointer marks where to write, a `fast` pointer scans — used to remove duplicates or move zeros in place.
lesson.analogy: Two friends searching a sorted bookshelf from both ends for two books whose prices add up to ₹500: if the pair is too expensive, the right friend steps to a cheaper book; too cheap, the left friend steps to a pricier one.

concepts.title: Why two pointers work on sorted input
concepts.body:
On a sorted array, the pair `(left, right)` with left at the start and right at the end gives you a decision at every step. For a target sum:

- `sum < target` → the only way to increase the sum is to move **left** right (right is already the biggest available).
- `sum > target` → move **right** left.

Each move **rules out a whole row of pairs** that can't work. For example, if `a[left] + a[right]` is too small, then `a[left]` paired with anything at or left of `right` is also too small — so `left` can never be part of the answer and you discard it. That's why one pass of O(n) is enough instead of checking all n² pairs.

**3Sum** builds on this: fix the first number with a loop, then run two pointers on the rest — O(n²) total, after an O(n log n) sort. Skip equal neighbours to avoid duplicate triplets.

concepts.title: The three shapes of two-pointer problems
concepts.body:
| Shape | Pointers | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Opposite ends**, moving inward | `left = 0`, `right = n − 1` | Two Sum II, 3Sum, Container With Most Water, Valid Palindrome |
| **Same direction**, read and write | `read` scans, `write` marks the next slot | Remove Duplicates, Move Zeroes, Remove Element |
| **Fast and slow** | one moves 1 step, the other 2 | middle of a linked list, cycle detection, Happy Number |

A fourth variant runs pointers over **two different arrays**: merging two sorted arrays, checking if one string is a subsequence of another, finding the intersection of two sorted lists.

Spotting the shape is most of the work. Ask: *is the input sorted (or can I sort it)? Do I need pairs? Am I asked to modify in place?*

concepts.title: Container With Most Water: proving the greedy move
concepts.body:
Given heights, pick two lines that hold the most water: area = `min(h[l], h[r]) × (r − l)`.

Start with the widest container (`l = 0`, `r = n − 1`). Which pointer should move? **Always move the shorter line.**

Why it's safe: suppose `h[l] < h[r]`. Any container using `l` with a line closer than `r` has **less width** and its height is still capped at `h[l]` (the min can't exceed `h[l]`). So every remaining container that uses `l` is worse than the one we just measured — we can drop `l` without missing the answer. Moving the taller line instead could never help, because the shorter one still caps the height.

This kind of argument — *"every option I'm throwing away is no better than one I've already seen"* — is exactly what interviewers want to hear when you use two pointers or greedy.

concepts.title: Read/write pointers for in-place filtering
concepts.body:
To remove items in place while keeping order, scan with `read` and copy keepers to `write`:

```python
def remove_duplicates(nums):          # nums is sorted
    write = 1
    for read in range(1, len(nums)):
        if nums[read] != nums[write - 1]:
            nums[write] = nums[read]
            write += 1
    return write                       # new length
```

Invariant: `nums[:write]` always holds the answer so far. Each element is read once → O(n), O(1) space.

Variation: *"allow at most two duplicates"* → compare with `nums[write - 2]` instead of `nums[write - 1]`. *Move Zeroes* swaps instead of copying so the zeroes end up at the back.

topics.revision_note_md:
## Pattern 3 — Sliding Window

**Core idea:** maintain a contiguous window `[left, right]` over an array or string. Instead of recomputing a property (sum, character count) from scratch for every subarray, update it incrementally — add what enters on the right, remove what leaves on the left.

**Decision trigger:** problem asks for a contiguous subarray or substring (not any subset), with a condition on its sum, character frequency, or distinctness.

**Two flavors:**
- **Fixed-size window** — window size `k` is given. Slide one step at a time, O(1) update per step.
- **Variable-size window** — window grows and shrinks based on a condition. `right` expands via a for-loop, `left` shrinks via a `while` loop (not `if`) — one expansion can require multiple shrinks.

items.title: Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K
hints: Compute sum of first k elements.
Slide window right by adding arr[i] and subtracting arr[i-k].
items.explanation: Fixed size sliding window of size k.
items.python:
def maximumSumSubarray(k: int, arr: list[int]) -> int:
    window_sum = sum(arr[:k])
    max_sum = window_sum
    for i in range(k, len(arr)):
        window_sum += arr[i] - arr[i - k]
        max_sum = max(max_sum, window_sum)
    return max_sum

items.title: Maximum Average Subarray I
hints: Find maximum sum of window of size k.
Divide max sum by k.
items.explanation: Fixed window of size k. Return max sum divided by k.
items.python:
def findMaxAverage(nums: list[int], k: int) -> float:
    curr = sum(nums[:k])
    max_s = curr
    for i in range(k, len(nums)):
        curr += nums[i] - nums[i - k]
        max_s = max(max_s, curr)
    return max_s / k

def checkInclusion(s1: str, s2: str) -> bool:
    if len(s1) > len(s2): return False
    c1, c2 = [0]*26, [0]*26
    for i in range(len(s1)):
        c1[ord(s1[i]) - 97] += 1
        c2[ord(s2[i]) - 97] += 1
    if c1 == c2: return True

items.explanation: Variable sliding window maintaining frequency counts of target string t.
items.python:
def minWindow(s: str, t: str) -> str:
    if not t or not s: return ''
    from collections import Counter
    dict_t = Counter(t)
    required = len(dict_t)
    l, r = 0, 0
    formed = 0
    window_counts = {}
    ans = (float('inf'), None, None)
    while r < len(s):
        character = s[r]
        window_counts[character] = window_counts.get(character, 0) + 1
        if character in dict_t and window_counts[character] == dict_t[character]:
            formed += 1
        while l <= r and formed == required:
            character = s[l]
            if r - l + 1 < ans[0]:
                ans = (r - l + 1, l, r)
            window_counts[character] -= 1
            if character in dict_t and window_counts[character] < dict_t[character]:
                formed -= 1
            l += 1
        r += 1
    return '' if ans[0] == float('inf') else s[ans[1]:ans[2] + 1]

lesson.simple:
A sliding window is a **range [left, right]** that moves across an array or string. Instead of recomputing every subarray from scratch, you **add the new element on the right and remove the old one on the left**.

- **Fixed size k**: slide one step at a time — add one, remove one.
- **Variable size**: grow `right` every step; while the window breaks the rule, shrink from `left`.
lesson.analogy: Looking at a long train through a window that shows 3 coaches. As the train moves, one coach enters and one leaves — you don't recount all three every time.

concepts.title: What a window is and why it's O(n)
concepts.body:
A **window** is a contiguous range `[left, right]` of an array or string. Instead of recomputing every subarray from scratch (O(n²) or worse), you **slide** the window: add the item entering on the right, remove the item leaving on the left, and update your answer.

Even with a `while` loop inside the `for` loop, the total work is **O(n)**: `right` moves forward n times and `left` moves forward at most n times in total. Neither pointer ever moves back. This "each pointer moves at most n times" argument is how you justify the complexity in an interview.

concepts.title: Fixed-size windows
concepts.body:
When the window size k is given (*"maximum sum of any k consecutive items"*, *"averages of subarrays of size k"*, *"find all anagrams of p in s"*):

```python
def max_sum_k(nums, k):
    window = sum(nums[:k])
    best = window
    for right in range(k, len(nums)):
        window += nums[right] - nums[right - k]   # add new, drop old
        best = max(best, window)
    return best
```

For anagram search, the window state is a **character count**; compare it with the target count (O(26)) each step, or keep a `matches` counter so the comparison is O(1).

concepts.title: Variable-size windows: expand, then shrink until valid
concepts.body:
When you need the **longest** or **shortest** window meeting a condition, use this template:

```text
for right in range(n):
    add nums[right] to the window state
    while the window is invalid:        # (or: while it's valid, for "shortest")
        remove nums[left]; left += 1
    update the answer
```

- **Longest substring without repeating characters** — invalid when a character count exceeds 1. Answer = max window length after shrinking.
- **Minimum size subarray sum ≥ target** — while the window *is* valid, record its length and shrink to try a smaller one.
- **Longest repeating character replacement** — valid while `window length − count of most frequent char ≤ k`.
- **Minimum window substring** — track how many required characters are satisfied; shrink while all are satisfied.

The window state is usually a **count map**, a running sum, or a "number of distinct items" counter.

concepts.title: When sliding window does NOT work
concepts.body:
Sliding window relies on a property: **growing the window moves the condition in one direction**, and shrinking moves it back. With only positive numbers, adding an item always increases the sum — so if the window's sum is too big, shrinking is the only fix.

With **negative numbers** that breaks: adding an item can decrease the sum, so you can't know whether to grow or shrink. *Subarray Sum Equals K* with negatives needs **prefix sums + a hash map** instead.

Other signs it's not a window problem:
- The items you choose **don't have to be contiguous** (that's a subsequence — often DP).
- The question is about **pairs at any distance** (two pointers on sorted data, or hashing).

A useful trick for *"exactly K distinct"*: count windows with **at most K** distinct minus windows with **at most K − 1**.

topics.revision_note_md:
## Linked List

- Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. No index access: reaching node k is O(k).
- **Dummy node** before the head removes edge cases when the head can change.
- **Reverse** with three pointers: prev, curr, next.
- **Slow/fast pointers** find the middle and detect cycles.

lesson.simple:
A linked list is a chain: each node knows only its value and **who comes next**. You can't jump to the 5th node — you walk there.

Almost every linked-list problem is solved with three tools:
1. **Dummy node** — a fake node before the head so you never special-case "what if the head changes?"
2. **Reverse** — flip each `next` pointer backwards using `prev`, `curr`, `next`.
3. **Slow & fast pointers** — fast moves 2 steps, slow moves 1: when fast reaches the end, slow is in the middle.
lesson.analogy: A treasure hunt where each clue tells you only where the next clue is. To reverse the hunt, at every clue you rewrite it to point back to the clue you just came from.

concepts.title: Nodes and pointers: what changes and what doesn't
concepts.body:
A linked list is a chain of **nodes**; each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. Unlike an array:

| Operation | Array | Linked list |
|---|---|---|
| Access item i | O(1) | O(i) — walk from the head |
| Insert/delete at a known node | O(n) shifting | **O(1)** pointer changes |
| Extra memory | none | one pointer per node |

Most bugs are about **losing a reference**. Before you change `node.next`, ask: *do I still have a way to reach the rest of the list?* That's why reversal saves `nxt = curr.next` before flipping the pointer.

Draw boxes and arrows for 3 nodes and update the arrows by hand — interviewers expect it, and it catches most mistakes.

concepts.title: The dummy (sentinel) node
concepts.body:
Many list operations need special handling when the **head itself** changes: deleting the first node, merging two lists, removing the n-th node from the end when n equals the length.

A **dummy node** placed before the head removes those special cases:

```python
def remove_elements(head, val):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    prev = dummy
    while prev.next:
        if prev.next.val == val:
            prev.next = prev.next.next      # unlink
        else:
            prev = prev.next
    return dummy.next                        # the real head, possibly changed
```

Now every real node has a predecessor, so one rule covers all cases. Use it whenever you're **building** a new list (merge, partition, add two numbers) or **deleting** nodes.

concepts.title: Fast and slow pointers
concepts.body:
Move `slow` one step and `fast` two steps at a time.

- **Middle of the list:** when `fast` reaches the end, `slow` is in the middle. (For even length, the loop condition decides whether you get the first or second middle.)
- **Cycle detection (Floyd):** if there's a cycle, `fast` laps `slow` and they meet; if `fast` hits `None`, there's no cycle.
- **Start of the cycle:** after they meet, move one pointer back to the head and advance both **one step at a time**; they meet at the cycle's entrance.

**Why the entrance trick works:** say the distance from head to the entrance is a, and they meet b steps inside a cycle of length c. Slow walked a + b; fast walked twice that, 2(a + b), which is a + b plus some whole laps: a + b = k·c. So a = k·c − b: walking a steps from the meeting point lands exactly on the entrance — the same as walking a steps from the head.

concepts.title: Reversal as a building block
concepts.body:
Iterative reversal (prev, curr, save next, flip, move) is O(n) time and O(1) space. It's the core of several harder problems:

- **Palindrome linked list:** find the middle, reverse the second half, compare the two halves, then (politely) reverse it back.
- **Reorder list** (L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln−1 …): find the middle, reverse the second half, merge the two halves alternately.
- **Reverse nodes in k-group:** count k nodes; if there are k, reverse that segment and reconnect it to the previous segment's tail; otherwise leave the rest as is.
- **Add two numbers** stored in forward order: reverse both, add digit by digit with a carry, reverse the result (or use stacks).

Recursive reversal also works but uses O(n) stack space — mention that trade-off.

## Pattern 7 — In-place Reversal of a Linked List

**Core idea:** reverse pointer directions as you walk — keep a `prev`, `curr`, and `next` pointer, update `curr.next = prev` at each step, then advance all three. No extra space needed.

**Decision trigger:** any problem asking you to reverse a linked list (or part of one) without using extra memory.

items.title: Reverse a Linked List
hints: Maintain prev, curr, next pointers.
curr.next = prev, then advance prev = curr, curr = next.
items.explanation: Iterative three-pointer in-place reversal.
items.python:
def reverseList(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt
    return prev

hints: Navigate to left-1 position.

Reconnect head and tail of reversed segment.
items.explanation: In-place partial sub-list reversal.
items.python:
def reverseBetween(head, left: int, right: int):
    if not head or left == right: return head
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    prev = dummy
    for _ in range(left - 1): prev = prev.next
    curr = prev.next
    for _ in range(right - left):
        temp = curr.next
        curr.next = temp.next
        temp.next = prev.next
        prev.next = temp
    return dummy.next

## Pattern 2 — Fast & Slow Pointers (Floyd's Algorithm)

**Core idea:** two pointers on a linked list or sequence, one moving at 2× the speed of the other. If a cycle exists, the fast pointer will lap the slow one and they'll meet. If not, fast simply reaches the end.

**Decision trigger:** linked list problems involving cycles, finding the k-th node from the end, or the middle node. Also applies to "happy number" style problems where you follow a numeric sequence and check for a loop.

    def get_next(i, is_forward):
        direction = nums[i] >= 0
        if is_forward != direction: return -1
        next_idx = (i + nums[i]) % n
        if next_idx < 0: next_idx += n
        if next_idx == i: return -1
        return next_idx
    for i in range(n):
        is_forward = nums[i] >= 0
        slow = fast = i
        while True:
            slow = get_next(slow, is_forward)
            fast = get_next(fast, is_forward)
            if fast != -1:
                fast = get_next(fast, is_forward)
            if slow == -1 or fast == -1: break
            if slow == fast: return True
    return False

## Pattern 12 — Recursion & Backtracking

**Core idea:** explore all possibilities by making a choice, recursing into the result, and then *undoing* that choice (backtracking) before trying the next option. The call stack maintains your history so you can cleanly undo.

**Decision trigger:** "generate all possible," "find all combinations/permutations/subsets," or "is there any valid arrangement?" — any problem where you need to explore a decision tree.

lesson.simple:
Recursion is a function that **calls itself on a smaller version of the problem** until it reaches a case small enough to answer directly (the **base case**).

Backtracking is recursion that **tries a choice, explores, then undoes the choice** — used to generate subsets, permutations and combinations.

Two questions for every recursive function:
1. What is the smallest input I can answer directly? (base case)
2. If a smaller call gives me the answer, how do I build mine from it?
lesson.analogy: Russian dolls: to count the dolls, open one and ask "how many are inside this smaller doll?" — until you reach the tiny doll that doesn't open (base case).

concepts.title: How recursion runs: the call stack
concepts.body:
Each call gets its own **frame** on the call stack with its own local variables. The function keeps calling itself on smaller inputs until it hits the **base case**, then the frames return one by one, each finishing its own work.

```python
def factorial(n):
    if n <= 1:          # base case
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)
```
`factorial(4)` waits for `factorial(3)`, which waits for `factorial(2)`… then `1` returns and the multiplications happen on the way back: 2, 6, 24.

Recursion depth costs **O(depth) memory**. Python's default limit is about 1,000 frames, so very deep recursion (a linked list of 10⁵ nodes, a long path in a grid) needs an iterative version or a raised limit.

**Trust the recursion:** don't trace every level in your head. Assume the smaller call returns the right answer and only check that you combine it correctly and that the base case is right.

concepts.title: The backtracking template: choose, explore, un-choose
concepts.body:
Backtracking explores a **decision tree**. At each level you make a choice, recurse, then undo the choice so the next option starts from a clean state.

```python
def backtrack(state, choices):
    if is_complete(state):
        results.append(state.copy())      # copy! state keeps changing
        return
    for choice in choices:
        if not valid(state, choice):
            continue                       # prune
        state.add(choice)                  # choose
        backtrack(state, next_choices)     # explore
        state.remove(choice)               # un-choose
```

Three families use it:
- **Subsets** — at each index, include or exclude: 2ⁿ results.
- **Permutations** — pick any unused item for the next slot: n! results; track a `used` array.
- **Combinations / combination sum** — choose items from index `start` onward so the same set isn't produced in a different order.

concepts.title: Handling duplicates and pruning
concepts.body:
**Duplicates in the input** (e.g. `[1, 2, 2]`) produce duplicate results unless you skip them. Sort first, then at each level skip a value equal to the previous one *at the same level*:

```python
for i in range(start, len(nums)):
    if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
        continue          # same choice already tried at this level
```

**Pruning** stops exploring branches that can't succeed, which is what makes backtracking fast enough in practice:
- Combination sum: stop the loop once the (sorted) candidate exceeds the remaining target.
- N-Queens: keep sets of used columns and diagonals (`r − c` and `r + c`) so each placement check is O(1).
- Word search: stop as soon as the next letter doesn't match; mark the cell visited and restore it afterwards.

concepts.title: Complexity of recursive solutions
concepts.body:
A practical way to estimate: **(number of calls) × (work per call)**.

- **Subsets:** 2ⁿ leaves, copying each result costs up to n → O(n · 2ⁿ).
- **Permutations:** n! results × n to copy → O(n · n!).
- **Naive Fibonacci:** each call makes two more → about 2ⁿ calls. Many calls repeat the same argument — that's the signal to **memoise**, which turns it into DP with only n distinct calls.
- **Divide and conquer** (merge sort): use the recursion tree — log n levels × n work per level.

Space is the **maximum depth** of the recursion plus whatever you store. For subsets and permutations that's O(n) for the current path (not counting the output).

def subsets(nums):
    result, current = [], []

    def backtrack(i):
        if i == len(nums):              # base case
            result.append(current[:])   # copy!
            return
        current.append(nums[i])         # choose
        backtrack(i + 1)                # explore
        current.pop()                   # un-choose
        backtrack(i + 1)                # explore without it

    backtrack(0)
    return result

## Pattern 8 — Stack

**Core idea:** use a stack when you need to access the "most recently seen" element that hasn't been resolved yet — common for matching pairs (brackets), finding the next greater/smaller element, or tracking running context while scanning.

**Decision trigger:** "next greater element," "balanced brackets," "undo last action," monotonic sequence problems, or any problem where the answer for the current element depends on something you recently passed but haven't finished processing.

lesson.simple:
A **stack** is last-in-first-out (LIFO) — like a pile of plates. A **queue** is first-in-first-out (FIFO) — like a ticket line.

Stacks shine when you need to **remember things and come back to the most recent one**: matching brackets, undo, and the famous **monotonic stack** for "next greater element" problems. Queues shine for **processing in arrival order**, especially BFS.
lesson.analogy: Browser back button is a stack (last page first). A printer queue is a queue (first job first).

concepts.title: When a stack is the right tool
concepts.body:
A stack lets you **remember things and come back to the most recent one first**. Reach for it when the problem has **nesting** or **"most recent unmatched"** structure:

- **Brackets** — push opening brackets, pop on a closing one and check it matches. Valid at the end only if the stack is empty.
- **Undo / back button / browser history.**
- **Expression evaluation** — Reverse Polish Notation: push numbers, pop two when you see an operator, push the result.
- **Simplify a file path** — split by `/`, push names, pop on `..`, ignore `.`.
- **Decode strings** like `3[a2[c]]` — push the current state at `[`, combine at `]`.
- **Iterative DFS** — replace recursion with an explicit stack.

Every push and pop is O(1). Python: use a list with `append` / `pop`. JS: an array with `push` / `pop`.

concepts.title: Monotonic stack: next greater / smaller element
concepts.body:
A **monotonic stack** keeps its items in increasing or decreasing order. When a new item breaks the order, you pop — and **each pop is an answer**.

*Next greater element:* walk left to right, keeping a stack of indices whose next greater element you haven't found yet (their values are decreasing). When `nums[i]` is bigger than the top, the top's answer is `nums[i]`; pop and repeat.

Why it's O(n): each index is pushed once and popped at most once.

| Want | Stack keeps values | Pop when new value is |
|---|---|---|
| next greater | decreasing | greater than top |
| next smaller | increasing | smaller than top |
| previous greater/smaller | same, but read the top *before* pushing | — |

Applications: **Daily Temperatures** (distance to next warmer day), **Stock Span**, **Largest Rectangle in Histogram** (for each bar, the nearest smaller bar on each side bounds its rectangle), **Trapping Rain Water** (stack version).

concepts.title: Queues, deques and the sliding window maximum
concepts.body:
A **queue** is first-in-first-out. Use `collections.deque` in Python (`append`, `popleft` are O(1)); in JS, an array with a moving head index (avoid `shift()`, which is O(n)).

A **deque** (double-ended queue) allows O(1) adds and removes at both ends, which enables the **monotonic deque**:

*Sliding window maximum:* keep indices in the deque with **decreasing values**. For each new index:
1. Pop from the back while the back's value ≤ the new value (they can never be the maximum again).
2. Push the new index.
3. Pop from the front if it's outside the window.
4. The front is the current window's maximum.

Each index enters and leaves once → O(n), instead of O(n·k) for scanning each window.

concepts.title: Designing stack/queue classes
concepts.body:
Classic design questions test whether you can keep extra information in sync:

- **Min Stack** (get min in O(1)): push `(value, min_so_far)` pairs, or keep a second stack of minimums. The min after a pop is simply the previous pair's min.
- **Queue using two stacks:** push onto `in_stack`; when popping, if `out_stack` is empty, move everything from `in_stack` to `out_stack` (reversing the order). Each item moves at most once → O(1) amortised.
- **Stack using queues:** after each push, rotate the queue so the newest item is at the front.

Always state the complexity of each method, and whether it's worst-case or amortised.

## Pattern 13 — Trees

**Core idea:** trees are recursively defined — every subtree is also a tree. Most tree problems are solved by asking "what do I need from the left subtree? From the right? What do I return to my parent?" and expressing that as a recursive function.

**Sub-patterns:** traversal order matters (inorder, preorder, postorder, level-order) depending on what you're computing. Level-order uses a queue (BFS). The rest use recursion (DFS).

lesson.simple:
A binary tree is a family tree where each node has at most two children: left and right. Almost every tree problem is solved by **visiting nodes** in one of two ways:

- **DFS (depth-first)** — go deep with recursion: preorder (node, left, right), inorder (left, node, right), postorder (left, right, node).
- **BFS (breadth-first)** — level by level with a queue.

The recursive mindset: *assume the function already works for the left and right subtrees; combine their answers.* Height = 1 + max(height(left), height(right)).
lesson.analogy: A company org chart: to count all employees under a manager, ask each direct report for their team size and add 1 for the manager. That's postorder DFS.

concepts.title: Tree vocabulary you'll use in every answer
concepts.body:
- **Root** — the top node. **Leaf** — a node with no children.
- **Depth** of a node — edges from the root to it. **Height** of a tree — the longest root-to-leaf path.
- **Binary tree** — each node has at most two children (left, right).
- **Balanced** — height is O(log n). A tree where every node has only one child is really a linked list: height O(n).
- **Complete** — every level is full except possibly the last, which fills from the left (that's how heaps are stored in arrays).

Why height matters: most tree algorithms cost **O(n)** to visit everything, but recursive ones use **O(h)** stack space, and BST operations cost **O(h)** time. So "O(log n) if balanced, O(n) worst case" is the honest answer.
