concepts.title: The four traversals and when to use each
concepts.body:
| Traversal | Order | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| **Pre-order** | node, left, right | copying/serialising a tree, building paths from the root |
| **In-order** | left, node, right | BSTs — visits values in sorted order |
| **Post-order** | left, right, node | anything that needs children's answers first: height, diameter, deleting a tree |
| **Level-order (BFS)** | level by level with a queue | level averages, right-side view, minimum depth, zig-zag |

Pre-, in- and post-order are all **DFS**; they differ only in *when* you process the node relative to its children. Recursive versions are 3 lines each. Iterative versions use a stack — in-order is the one worth practising: push all left children, pop, visit, then move to the right child.

concepts.title: Thinking recursively: what does each node return?
concepts.body:
Most tree problems are solved by deciding **what a node should return to its parent**, then combining the children's results.

- **Maximum depth:** return `1 + max(left, right)`; empty tree returns 0.
- **Is balanced:** return the height, or −1 to signal "unbalanced" so you don't recompute heights (O(n) instead of O(n²)).
- **Diameter** (longest path between any two nodes): each node returns its height, but along the way updates a global best with `left_height + right_height`. The path through a node uses both sides; the value returned to the parent can use only one.
- **Maximum path sum:** same shape — return the best single-branch sum (ignore negative branches with `max(0, …)`), update a global best with the "bent" path through the node.

This "return one thing, track another globally" pattern solves a big group of hard tree questions.

concepts.title: Lowest common ancestor and paths
concepts.body:
The **lowest common ancestor (LCA)** of p and q is the deepest node that has both under it.

For a general binary tree, recurse:
```python
def lca(node, p, q):
    if not node or node is p or node is q:
        return node
    left, right = lca(node.left, p, q), lca(node.right, p, q)
    if left and right:
        return node             # p and q are on different sides
    return left or right        # both on one side (or not found)
```
O(n) time, O(h) space.

Related path problems:
- **Path sum** — pass the remaining target down; check at leaves.
- **All root-to-leaf paths** — backtracking: append the node, recurse, pop.
- **Path Sum III** (paths that can start anywhere) — prefix sums on the root-to-node path with a hash map, exactly like the array version.

concepts.title: BFS level by level
concepts.body:
Level-order traversal uses a **queue**. The trick for working one level at a time is to read the queue's length *before* processing:

```python
from collections import deque
queue = deque([root])
while queue:
    for _ in range(len(queue)):        # exactly the nodes on this level
        node = queue.popleft()
        ...                             # process
        if node.left: queue.append(node.left)
        if node.right: queue.append(node.right)
    # end of a level here
```

From this one loop: **right-side view** (last node of each level), **level averages**, **zig-zag order** (reverse every other level), **minimum depth** (first leaf you meet), **connect next pointers**. BFS uses O(width) memory — up to n/2 for the last level of a full tree.

## BST

- For every node: all values in the **left subtree < node < all values in the right subtree**.
- Search/insert: go left or right → O(h); h = log n if balanced, n if skewed.
- **Inorder traversal of a BST is sorted.**

lesson.simple:
A Binary Search Tree is a binary tree with one rule: **smaller values go left, bigger go right** — at every node. That rule turns searching into binary search: at each node you throw away half the tree.

The magic fact to remember: **an inorder traversal (left, node, right) visits BST values in sorted order.** Many BST questions are just "do inorder and use the sorted order".
lesson.analogy: A dictionary game: you open the middle; if your word comes earlier you only look at the left half, otherwise the right half. A BST stores that decision at every node.

concepts.title: The BST property and what it buys you
concepts.body:
In a **binary search tree**, for every node: everything in the **left subtree is smaller**, everything in the **right subtree is larger**. Not just the direct children — the *whole* subtree.

That gives you binary search on a tree: at each node, go left or right and discard the other half. Search, insert and delete cost **O(h)**: O(log n) when balanced, O(n) when the tree degenerates (inserting sorted data into a plain BST makes a linked list).

Production systems use **self-balancing** trees (red-black, AVL) that guarantee O(log n) — for example Java's `TreeMap` and C++'s `std::map`. In interviews you're rarely asked to write rotations, but you should know why balancing matters.

concepts.title: In-order traversal gives sorted order
concepts.body:
Because left < node < right everywhere, an **in-order traversal visits values in increasing order**. This single fact solves many problems:

- **Validate a BST** — in-order values must be strictly increasing (or pass `(low, high)` bounds down the recursion).
- **K-th smallest** — do an in-order traversal and stop at the k-th node: O(h + k).
- **Two Sum in a BST** — in-order into a sorted list, then two pointers (or a set during traversal).
- **Recover a BST** where two nodes were swapped — find the two places where the in-order sequence decreases.
- **Convert a sorted array to a balanced BST** — the reverse: pick the middle as the root, recurse on the halves.

concepts.title: Deleting a node: the three cases
concepts.body:
Deleting is the one BST operation with real case analysis:

1. **Leaf** — just remove it.
2. **One child** — replace the node with its child.
3. **Two children** — find the **in-order successor** (the smallest node in the right subtree: go right once, then left as far as possible). Copy its value into the node, then delete the successor from the right subtree (it has at most one child, so it falls into case 1 or 2).

```python
def delete(root, key):
    if not root: return None
    if key < root.val: root.left = delete(root.left, key)
    elif key > root.val: root.right = delete(root.right, key)
    else:
        if not root.left: return root.right
        if not root.right: return root.left
        succ = root.right
        while succ.left: succ = succ.left
        root.val = succ.val
        root.right = delete(root.right, succ.val)
    return root
```

concepts.body:
The BST order lets you skip whole subtrees:

- **LCA in a BST** — if both p and q are smaller than the node, go left; if both are larger, go right; otherwise the current node is the split point, so it's the LCA. O(h), no need to search both sides.

## Pattern 5 — Prefix Sum

**Core idea:** precompute a running cumulative sum so any subarray sum `[i, j]` is answered in O(1) as `prefix[j+1] - prefix[i]`, instead of scanning the range each time.

**Decision trigger:** problem asks "how many subarrays sum to exactly K?" or involves range sum queries, or a condition on subarray sums that you'd normally re-scan to evaluate. Prefix sum also pairs with a HashMap to count how many times a specific prefix sum has appeared so far.

items.python:
def productExceptSelf(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    res = [1] * n
    prefix = 1
    for i in range(n):
        res[i] = prefix
        prefix *= nums[i]
    suffix = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        res[i] *= suffix
        suffix *= nums[i]
    return res

topics.revision_note_md:
## Pattern 4 — Kadane's Algorithm

**Core idea:** at every index, decide — is it better to extend the running subarray that ended at the previous element, or start fresh from here? This local decision at every step leads to the global maximum subarray sum in O(n).

**Decision trigger:** problem asks for the maximum (or minimum) sum/product of a contiguous subarray. If you see "subarray" and "max/min value," Kadane is almost always the answer before any other approach.

**Core formula:**
```
current = max(nums[i], current + nums[i])
result  = max(result, current)
```

hints: Track both max_product and min_product due to negative numbers.
When encountering negative number, swap max_product and min_product.
items.explanation: Dual tracking of min and max products.
items.python:
def maxProduct(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    res = max_p = min_p = nums[0]
    for x in nums[1:]:
        if x < 0: max_p, min_p = min_p, max_p
        max_p = max(x, max_p * x)
        min_p = min(x, min_p * x)
        res = max(res, max_p)
    return res

hints: Max circular sum is either max_kadane OR (total_sum - min_kadane).
Handle edge case where all numbers are negative.
items.explanation: Combine normal Kadane (max sum) with inverted Kadane (min sum).
items.python:
def maxSubarraySumCircular(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    total = sum(nums)
    curr_max = max_sum = nums[0]
    curr_min = min_sum = nums[0]
    for x in nums[1:]:
        curr_max = max(x, curr_max + x)
        max_sum = max(max_sum, curr_max)
        curr_min = min(x, curr_min + x)
        min_sum = min(min_sum, curr_min)
    if max_sum < 0: return max_sum
    return max(max_sum, total - min_sum)

## Pattern 6 — Merge Intervals

**Core idea:** sort intervals by start time. Then walk through them — if the current interval overlaps the previous one (current.start ≤ prev.end), merge by extending the end. Otherwise start a new group.

**Decision trigger:** problem involves time ranges, meeting schedules, calendar slots, or any "do these ranges overlap / merge" question.

items.python:
def insert(intervals: list[list[int]], newInterval: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
    res = []
    i = 0
    n = len(intervals)
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < newInterval[0]:
        res.append(intervals[i])
        i += 1
    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= newInterval[1]:
        newInterval[0] = min(newInterval[0], intervals[i][0])
        newInterval[1] = max(newInterval[1], intervals[i][1])
        i += 1
    res.append(newInterval)
    while i < n:
        res.append(intervals[i])
        i += 1
    return res

lesson.simple:
A **heap** (priority queue) is a box that always hands you the **smallest** (or largest) item quickly. Adding an item and removing the top both take **O(log n)**; peeking at the top is **O(1)**.

You don't need to sort everything when you only care about *the best few*. That is the whole trick: **"top K", "K-th largest", "closest K", "merge K sorted"** → think heap.

The surprising rule: to keep the **K largest**, use a **min-heap of size K**. The smallest of your K champions sits on top, so it's the one you kick out when a bigger number arrives.
lesson.analogy: A hospital emergency room. Patients don't get seen in arrival order — the most urgent one is always next. New patients slot in by urgency without re-sorting the whole waiting room.

concepts.title: How a binary heap is stored
concepts.body:
A heap is a **complete binary tree** stored in a plain array — no pointers. For the node at index i:
- left child at `2i + 1`, right child at `2i + 2`
- parent at `(i − 1) // 2`

The **heap property** (min-heap): every parent ≤ its children. So the minimum is always at index 0. Note that siblings aren't ordered and the array isn't sorted — only the parent/child relationship is guaranteed.

Because the tree is complete, its height is ⌊log₂ n⌋. That's where every O(log n) in heap operations comes from.

concepts.title: Push, pop and heapify, step by step
concepts.body:
**Push (sift up):** put the new item at the end of the array, then swap it with its parent while it's smaller than the parent. At most log n swaps.

**Pop (sift down):** remove the root, move the last item to the root, then swap it with its **smaller child** while it's bigger than that child. At most log n swaps.

**Heapify (build a heap from n items):** sift down every non-leaf node, starting from the last one and moving to the root. Surprisingly this is **O(n)**, not O(n log n): most nodes are near the bottom and sift down only a step or two. Python: `heapq.heapify(list)`.

**Heap sort** = heapify, then pop n times: O(n log n), in place, not stable. Rarely asked to write, but good to mention.

concepts.title: Top-K, K-th largest and why a size-K heap
concepts.body:
To keep the **K largest** items of a stream, keep a **min-heap of size K**. Its root is the smallest of your current top K — the weakest champion. When a new item arrives:
- push it;
- if the heap grows beyond K, pop the root.

After processing everything, the heap holds the K largest and the root is the **K-th largest**. Cost: O(n log K) time, O(K) space.

Compare the options out loud:

| Approach | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| Sort everything | O(n log n) | O(n) or in place |
| Max-heap of all items, pop K times | O(n + K log n) | O(n) |
| **Min-heap of size K** | **O(n log K)** | **O(K)** — works on streams |
| Quickselect | O(n) average, O(n²) worst | in place |

For *Top K Frequent*, count with a hash map first, then run the size-K heap over `(count, value)` pairs. **Bucket sort by frequency** gives O(n).

concepts.title: Two heaps and merging K sorted streams
concepts.body:
**Median of a data stream:** keep a **max-heap for the lower half** and a **min-heap for the upper half**.
1. Push the new number into the lower half (max-heap), then move the lower half's maximum to the upper half — this keeps every lower item ≤ every upper item.
2. If the upper half becomes bigger, move its minimum back.
3. Median = top of the lower half (odd count) or the average of both tops (even count).
Each insert is O(log n); reading the median is O(1).

**Merge K sorted lists:** push the head of each list into a min-heap of `(value, list_index, node)`. Pop the smallest, append it to the result, push that node's next. The heap never holds more than K items → **O(N log K)** for N total nodes. The same idea finds the **smallest range covering K lists** and **K-th smallest in a sorted matrix**.

Python tip: heaps compare tuples element by element, so include a tiebreaker (an index) before objects that can't be compared.

topics.name: Greedy Algorithms
topics.description: Make the locally best choice and never look back — when that works and how to prove it.
topics.revision_note_md:
## Greedy

- Make the **locally best choice** at each step and never undo it.
- Only correct when you can argue *"taking the best now never hurts later"* (an exchange argument).
- Very often: **sort first** (by end time, by ratio, by size), then one pass.
- If a counter-example breaks your greedy rule → it's probably DP.

lesson.simple:
**Greedy** means: at every step, take the choice that looks best *right now*, and never go back.

It's the simplest strategy, and it's often wrong — so the skill is knowing **when it's safe**. It's safe when you can say *"picking the best option now can't block a better answer later"*.

Most greedy problems follow one recipe: **sort the items by the right key, then walk once making the obvious choice.** For intervals the right key is usually the **end time**.
lesson.analogy: Paying ₹87 with ₹50, ₹20, ₹10, ₹5, ₹2, ₹1 coins: always hand over the biggest coin that fits (50, 20, 10, 5, 2). With Indian coins this greedy is always optimal. With weird coins like {1, 3, 4} for 6 it fails (4+1+1 vs 3+3) — that's when you need DP.

concepts.title: What makes a greedy choice safe
concepts.body:
Greedy algorithms build the answer one step at a time, always taking the choice that looks best now, and never reconsidering. They're correct only when two things hold:

1. **Greedy-choice property** — there's an optimal answer that starts with the greedy choice.
2. **Optimal substructure** — after making that choice, what's left is a smaller version of the same problem.

You prove the first with an **exchange argument**: take any optimal answer that doesn't make the greedy choice, swap in the greedy choice, and show the answer is no worse. If that swap always works, greedy is safe.

If you can't make that argument — or you find a small counter-example — the problem probably needs **dynamic programming**, which tries every choice instead of one.

concepts.title: Interval scheduling: why 'earliest end' wins
concepts.body:
*Pick the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals.* Candidates for the greedy rule: shortest first? earliest start? fewest overlaps? **Earliest end** is the one that's provably right.

Exchange argument: let the earliest-ending interval be g. Take any optimal schedule; its first interval f ends at or after g ends (g ends earliest of all). Replace f with g: g finishes no later, so it can't clash with anything that came after f. The schedule stays valid and has the same size. Repeat for the rest.

Counter-examples for the other rules:
- **Earliest start** fails on `[1, 10], [2, 3], [4, 5]` — it picks the long one and loses two.
- **Shortest first** fails on `[1, 5], [4, 7], [6, 10]` — it picks `[4, 7]` and blocks both others.

Related: *Non-overlapping Intervals* (remove = total − kept), *Minimum Arrows to Burst Balloons* (same greedy), *Meeting Rooms II* (a different question — count rooms with a min-heap of end times or a sweep line).

concepts.title: Reach-based greedy: Jump Game I and II
concepts.body:
**Jump Game I** — can you reach the last index? Track `farthest`, the furthest index reachable so far. At each index i: if `i > farthest`, you're stuck; otherwise `farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])`. It works because reachable indices always form a continuous prefix, so remembering the boundary is enough.

**Jump Game II** — the minimum number of jumps. Think of it as **BFS by levels without a queue**: all indices reachable with j jumps form a range `[start, end]`. While scanning that range, compute the furthest you can reach with one more jump. When `i` reaches `end`, you must jump: `jumps += 1`, `end = farthest`.

```python
jumps = end = farthest = 0
for i in range(len(nums) - 1):
    farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])
    if i == end:
        jumps += 1
        end = farthest
```
O(n) time, O(1) space.

concepts.title: Two-pass and sort-and-match greedy
concepts.body:
**Two passes** handle constraints from both sides. *Candy*: each child with a higher rating than a neighbour gets more candy than that neighbour.
1. Left to right: if `rating[i] > rating[i − 1]`, `candy[i] = candy[i − 1] + 1`.
2. Right to left: if `rating[i] > rating[i + 1]`, `candy[i] = max(candy[i], candy[i + 1] + 1)`.
One pass can't see the constraint coming from the other side.

**Sort and match** pairs two sorted lists greedily. *Assign Cookies*: sort children's greed and cookie sizes, give each child the smallest cookie that satisfies them. *Boats to Save People*: sort, pair the heaviest with the lightest if they fit together.

**Gas Station** is a classic "reset" greedy: if the running tank goes negative at station i, no station between the current start and i can be the start either — so jump the start to i + 1. If total gas ≥ total cost, a valid start exists.

## Graphs

- Store as an **adjacency list**: `graph[u] = [v, ...]`. Grids are graphs too (4 neighbours).

lesson.simple:
A **graph** is dots (nodes) connected by lines (edges): cities and roads, people and friendships, courses and prerequisites. A grid is a graph too — each cell connects to its 4 neighbours.

You only need four tools for most interviews:
1. **BFS** — explore in rings, nearest first. Gives the **shortest path** when every step costs the same.
2. **DFS** — go as deep as possible, then back up. Good for **counting islands/components** and **detecting cycles**.
3. **Topological sort** — order tasks so every prerequisite comes first (course schedule).
4. **Dijkstra** — shortest path when edges have **different (non-negative) costs**.

The one rule that prevents infinite loops: **mark a node visited when you add it.**
lesson.analogy: BFS is a ripple in a pond: it reaches everything 1 step away, then 2 steps, then 3. DFS is exploring a maze with one hand on the wall: go deep down one corridor before trying the next.

concepts.title: Representing a graph
concepts.body:
A graph has **vertices** (V) and **edges** (E). Edges can be **directed** (one-way, like course prerequisites) or **undirected** (two-way, like friendships), and **weighted** (cost, distance, time) or unweighted.

| Representation | Space | Check edge u–v | List neighbours |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Adjacency list** `graph[u] = [v, …]` | O(V + E) | O(degree) | O(degree) — fast |
| **Adjacency matrix** `m[u][v]` | O(V²) | O(1) | O(V) |
| **Edge list** `[(u, v, w), …]` | O(E) | O(E) | O(E) |

Use an adjacency list by default. Build it from an edge list with a `defaultdict(list)`, adding both directions for undirected graphs.

**Grids are implicit graphs:** each cell is a vertex, edges go to the 4 (or 8) neighbours. You don't build the graph — you generate neighbours on the fly with a directions list and a bounds check.

concepts.title: BFS vs DFS: what each guarantees
concepts.body:
**BFS** explores in rings using a queue: all nodes 1 edge away, then 2, then 3. So the first time BFS reaches a node, it's by the **fewest edges**. Use it for shortest paths in unweighted graphs and "minimum number of moves" puzzles. **Multi-source BFS** starts with many nodes in the queue at distance 0 — Rotten Oranges, distance to the nearest 0 in a matrix, walls and gates.

**DFS** follows one path as deep as possible, then backtracks (recursion or a stack). It doesn't give shortest paths, but it's natural for **exploring everything reachable**: counting islands/components, flood fill, detecting cycles, finding all paths, and topological order.

Both cost **O(V + E)**: each vertex is visited once and each edge examined once (twice for undirected). The `visited` set is what guarantees "once" — mark a node when you **add** it to the queue/stack, not when you take it out, or the same node gets added many times.

concepts.title: Cycle detection and topological sort
concepts.body:
**Undirected graph:** a cycle exists if DFS reaches an already-visited node that isn't the node it came from (its parent). Union-Find also works: an edge between two nodes already in the same set is a cycle.

**Directed graph:** "visited" isn't enough — use three colours: *unvisited*, *in the current path*, *done*. Reaching a node that's **in the current path** means a back edge, i.e. a cycle.

**Topological sort** orders a directed acyclic graph (DAG) so every edge goes from earlier to later — e.g. a valid course order.

**Kahn's algorithm (BFS):**
1. Count each node's **in-degree** (incoming edges).
2. Queue all nodes with in-degree 0 (no prerequisites).
3. Pop a node, add it to the order, decrement its neighbours' in-degrees; queue any that reach 0.
4. If the order has fewer than V nodes, the leftover nodes are stuck in a **cycle**.

The DFS alternative adds a node to the order **after** all its descendants finish, then reverses the list.

concepts.title: Shortest paths with weights: Dijkstra and friends
concepts.body:
When edges have different costs, BFS isn't enough. **Dijkstra's algorithm** works for **non-negative** weights:

1. `dist[start] = 0`; push `(0, start)` into a min-heap.
2. Pop the closest unfinished node u. If the popped distance is larger than `dist[u]`, it's a stale entry — skip it.
3. For each edge u → v with weight w: if `dist[u] + w < dist[v]`, update `dist[v]` and push `(dist[v], v)`.

Why it's correct: when a node is popped with the smallest distance, no other path can reach it more cheaply later — every other path would have to go through a node that's already at least as far, and weights can't be negative. That's exactly the assumption that **negative edges** break.

| Situation | Algorithm | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Unweighted | BFS | O(V + E) |
| Weights 0 or 1 | 0-1 BFS with a deque | O(V + E) |
| Non-negative weights | Dijkstra | O((V + E) log V) |
| Negative weights / at most K edges | Bellman-Ford (K + 1 rounds) | O(K · E) |
| All pairs, small V | Floyd–Warshall | O(V³) |

concepts.title: Minimum spanning trees
concepts.body:
A **minimum spanning tree (MST)** connects all vertices of a weighted undirected graph with the **smallest total edge weight** and no cycles (exactly V − 1 edges). Think: laying cable to connect every office as cheaply as possible.

- **Kruskal:** sort all edges by weight; add each edge if it connects two different components (check with **Union-Find**). O(E log E).
- **Prim:** grow the tree from any start vertex; repeatedly add the cheapest edge leaving the tree (min-heap). O(E log V).

Both are greedy, and both are correct because of the **cut property**: for any way of splitting the vertices into two groups, the cheapest edge crossing between them belongs to some MST.

Interview examples: *Min Cost to Connect All Points* (Prim is simpler for dense graphs), *Connecting Cities With Minimum Cost*.

Weighted shortest path (flights, network delay) → Dijkstra; with a stop limit → Bellman-Ford style BFS.
"Are these connected?" asked many times → Union-Find (next lesson).
mistakes: Marking visited when you *pop* instead of when you *push* — the same node enters the queue many times.
Using `list.pop(0)` (Python) or `shift()` (JS) as a queue — O(n) each; use deque or a head index.
Running Dijkstra with negative edge weights — it gives wrong answers.
Forgetting disconnected parts: loop over every node and start a new DFS/BFS if unvisited.
Deep recursion on a 1000×1000 grid — mention the recursion limit or use an explicit stack.
interview_tips: First say how you'll store the graph (adjacency list) and whether it's directed or weighted.
Pick the tool out loud: "Equal costs → BFS; weights → Dijkstra; dependencies → topological sort."
Complexity is always in V and E — say O(V + E), not O(n²), unless it's a dense matrix.

topics.name: Disjoint Set (Union-Find)
topics.description: Track connected groups with near-O(1) union and find — the tool for connectivity and Kruskal's MST.
topics.revision_note_md:
## Union-Find (Disjoint Set)

- `find(x)` → the leader (root) of x's group. `union(a, b)` → merge two groups.
- **Path compression** + **union by rank/size** → almost O(1) per operation.
- `find(a) == find(b)` before a union → the edge closes a **cycle**.
- Components = number of successful unions subtracted from n.
- Used in Kruskal's minimum spanning tree.

lesson.simple:
**Union-Find** keeps track of **groups**. It answers one question very fast: *are these two things in the same group?*

Every group has a **leader**. `find(x)` walks up to x's leader. `union(a, b)` makes one leader point to the other, merging the groups.

Two small tricks make it nearly O(1):
- **Path compression** — after finding the leader, point every node on the way directly at it.
- **Union by rank** — attach the shorter tree under the taller one.

If `find(a) == find(b)` *before* you join them, the edge a–b would make a **cycle**.
lesson.analogy: Friend circles at a college. Each circle has a captain. To check if two students are in the same circle, ask each "who's your captain?" When two circles become friends, one captain agrees to report to the other.

concepts.title: The idea: each group is a tree with a leader
concepts.body:
Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union, DSU) keeps a collection of **non-overlapping groups** and supports two operations:

- `find(x)` — which group is x in? Returns the group's **representative** (root).
- `union(a, b)` — merge the groups containing a and b.

Internally every group is a tree stored in a `parent` array. A root points to itself. `find` follows parent pointers up to the root; `union` points one root at the other.

Without optimisation the trees can become long chains, making `find` O(n). Two small tricks fix that.

concepts.title: Path compression and union by rank: why it's almost O(1)
concepts.body:
**Path compression:** during `find(x)`, point every node you passed directly at the root. The next `find` on any of them is one step.

**Union by rank (or size):** when merging, attach the **shorter** (or smaller) tree under the taller one, so trees stay shallow. Rank is an upper bound on height and only grows when two equal-rank trees merge.

With both, a sequence of m operations costs O(m · α(n)), where α is the inverse Ackermann function — it's **at most 4 for any n you'll ever see**. In an interview: *"effectively constant time per operation."*

Either trick alone already gives O(log n) per operation; together they're near-constant. Path *halving* (`parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]` while walking up) is a loop-friendly variant with the same guarantee.

concepts.title: Patterns Union-Find solves
concepts.body:
- **Counting components** as edges arrive: start with n components; each successful union reduces the count by one. (*Number of Provinces*, *Number of Operations to Make Network Connected*: you need components − 1 extra cables, and it's impossible if there are fewer than n − 1 edges.)
- **Cycle detection in undirected graphs:** if `find(a) == find(b)` before adding edge a–b, that edge closes a cycle (*Redundant Connection*).
- **Grouping by shared attributes:** union items that share something — accounts sharing an email (*Accounts Merge*), stones sharing a row or column, variables that must be equal (*Satisfiability of Equality Equations*).
- **Kruskal's MST:** sort edges, union if they join different components.
- **Grid connectivity** with cells added over time (*Number of Islands II*): map `(r, c)` to `r × cols + c`.

Mapping non-integer items (emails, names) to ids: give each a number the first time you see it with a dict.

concepts.title: Union-Find vs BFS/DFS: choosing
concepts.body:
| Situation | Better choice |
|---|---|
| The graph is given all at once and you need components once | BFS/DFS (simple, O(V + E)) |
| Edges arrive **one by one** and you query connectivity in between | **Union-Find** |
| You need the **path** or distance between nodes | BFS/DFS/Dijkstra |
| The graph is **directed** | BFS/DFS (Union-Find only models undirected connectivity) |
| You need to **remove** edges | Neither directly — often process removals in reverse as additions |

A common interview move: solve with DFS first, then mention that Union-Find handles the online / incremental version.

topics.revision_note_md:
## Dynamic Programming (Part 1)

1. **Define the state**: `dp[i]` = the answer for the first i items / ending at i.
2. **Recurrence**: how `dp[i]` is built from smaller states (try every choice).
3. **Base cases**.
4. **Order**: top-down (recursion + memo) or bottom-up (table).
5. **Space**: if `dp[i]` only needs the last 1–2 values, keep just those.

Classic 1D: Climbing Stairs, House Robber, Coin Change, LIS. Classic 2D: Unique Paths, LCS, Edit Distance, Knapsack.

hints: dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]

hints: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i])

def rob(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    rob1, rob2 = 0, 0
    for num in nums:
        temp = max(rob1 + num, rob2)
        rob1 = rob2
        rob2 = temp
    return rob2

lesson.simple:
**Dynamic programming (DP)** is recursion that **remembers its answers** so it never solves the same small problem twice.

If a brute-force recursion keeps asking the same question ("best answer from index 5?") again and again, store the answer the first time. That turns exponential time into polynomial time.

Every DP solution answers four questions:
1. **State** — what does `dp[i]` mean, in one sentence?
2. **Choice** — at step i, what can I do? (take it / skip it, which coin, which direction)
3. **Recurrence** — `dp[i]` = best over those choices, using smaller states.
4. **Base case** — the smallest inputs you can answer directly.

Write the recursion first, add a memo, and only then (if needed) convert it to a table.
lesson.analogy: Climbing a staircase and writing on each step how many ways there are to reach it. To fill step 10 you just add the numbers on steps 9 and 8 — you never re-walk the whole staircase.

concepts.title: Recognising a DP problem
concepts.body:
DP applies when a problem has two properties:

1. **Optimal substructure** — the best answer is built from best answers to smaller sub-problems (the best way to climb to step 10 comes from the best ways to step 9 and 8).
2. **Overlapping sub-problems** — the same sub-problem is needed many times. Naive recursion for Fibonacci computes `fib(3)` dozens of times.

Wording that usually means DP: **"number of ways"**, **"minimum/maximum cost"**, **"longest/shortest"**, **"is it possible"** — combined with choices at each step and an order you can process (left to right, smaller to larger).

If choices don't interact (taking the best now never hurts later) it may be greedy. If you need **all** the solutions themselves (not just how many), it's backtracking.

concepts.title: From recursion to memo to table: a worked path
concepts.body:
Take **Coin Change** (fewest coins to make `amount`).

**1. Brute-force recursion.** To make amount a, the last coin is some c; then make a − c.
```python
def best(a):
    if a == 0: return 0
    if a < 0: return inf
    return 1 + min(best(a - c) for c in coins)
```
Exponential, because `best(a)` is recomputed for the same a many times.

**2. Memoise.** Add `@cache`. Now each amount 0..A is solved once, each in O(len(coins)) → **O(A · C)**.

**3. Tabulate (bottom-up).** Fill `dp[0..A]` in increasing order so `dp[a − c]` is ready when you need it:
```python
dp = [0] + [inf] * amount
for a in range(1, amount + 1):
    for c in coins:
        if c <= a:
            dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1)
```
No recursion depth limit, and it's easy to see the order.

**4. Optimise space** if each state only needs the last row or last few values (House Robber → two variables).

concepts.title: Defining the state well
concepts.body:
The hardest step is choosing what `dp[...]` means. Write it as a **full sentence** before coding:

- *"dp[i] = the most money you can rob from the first i houses."*
- *"dp[i] = the length of the longest increasing subsequence that **ends at** index i."* (Note: "ends at", so the answer is `max(dp)`, not `dp[n − 1]`.)
- *"dp[i][j] = the LCS length of `a[:i]` and `b[:j]`."*
- *"dp[a] = true if amount a can be formed."*

Good states are **small** (one or two indices, maybe a small extra dimension like "holding a stock or not") and **complete** — they contain everything needed to make the next decision. If your recurrence needs information the state doesn't have, add a dimension.

Then write the **base cases** (empty prefix, amount 0, first row/column) and the **answer location**.

concepts.title: The common DP families
concepts.body:
| Family | State | Recurrence idea | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1D linear** | dp[i] over a prefix | combine dp[i−1], dp[i−2] | Climbing Stairs, House Robber, Decode Ways |
| **Unbounded choices** | dp[amount] | try every item, reuse allowed | Coin Change, Perfect Squares, Word Break |
| **LIS-style** | dp[i] ending at i | best over all j < i with a[j] < a[i] | LIS (O(n²), or O(n log n) with patience sorting) |
| **Grid** | dp[r][c] | from top and left | Unique Paths, Minimum Path Sum |
| **Two sequences** | dp[i][j] | match → diagonal; else best of top/left | LCS, Edit Distance |
| **0/1 knapsack** | dp[i][capacity] | skip item i or take it once | Partition Equal Subset Sum, Target Sum |

**Coin Change II (count combinations)** shows why loop order matters: loop over **coins outside, amounts inside** to count combinations (each set once); amounts outside, coins inside counts permutations (orders as different).

concepts.title: Two-sequence DP: LCS and Edit Distance
concepts.body:
For two strings a and b, let `dp[i][j]` describe the prefixes `a[:i]` and `b[:j]`. Row 0 and column 0 represent empty prefixes.

**LCS:** if `a[i−1] == b[j−1]`, that character extends the LCS of the shorter prefixes: `dp[i−1][j−1] + 1`. Otherwise drop one character from either string: `max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1])`.

**Edit Distance** (insert, delete, replace, each costs 1):
- characters equal → `dp[i−1][j−1]` (no cost)
- otherwise `1 + min(dp[i−1][j] (delete), dp[i][j−1] (insert), dp[i−1][j−1] (replace))`
- base cases: `dp[i][0] = i` (delete everything), `dp[0][j] = j` (insert everything)

Both are O(m·n) time. Since each row only needs the previous row, space drops to O(min(m, n)) with two rows. To **reconstruct** the actual subsequence or edits, keep the full table and walk back from `dp[m][n]`.

mistakes: Jumping straight to a table without defining what dp[i] means — the recurrence then becomes guesswork.
Wrong base cases (dp[0] for Coin Change must be 0, not infinity).
Off-by-one between string index and dp index in 2D problems (dp[i] uses a[i-1]).
Using a mutable default or a global memo that leaks between test cases.
Mixing up the loop order for counting combinations vs permutations in coin problems.

topics.revision_note_md:
## Trie

- Each node has children for the next character and an `end` flag.
- Insert/search a word of length L: O(L), independent of how many words are stored.
- Great for prefix queries and searching many words at once.

lesson.simple: A trie stores words letter by letter in a tree, so words that share a prefix share a path. Checking "does any word start with 'app'?" is just walking three nodes.
key_points: Node = dict/array of children + is_end flag.
Insert and search are O(word length).
startsWith only checks the path exists.
Word Search II: build a trie of the words, then DFS the board once.

topics.name: Bit Manipulation
topics.description: AND, OR, XOR and shifts — tricks for single numbers, counting bits and subsets.
topics.revision_note_md:
## Bits

- `x & 1` → odd? `x >> 1` → divide by 2. `x & (x - 1)` → clears the lowest set bit.
- **XOR**: a ^ a = 0, a ^ 0 = a → finds the unique number among pairs.
- A bitmask of n bits represents a subset of n items.

lesson.simple: Computers store numbers as bits. A few bit operations replace whole loops: XOR cancels pairs, `x & (x-1)` removes one set bit, and shifting multiplies or divides by 2.
key_points: XOR all numbers to find the one without a pair.
Count set bits with x &= x - 1 until zero.
Power of two: x > 0 and x & (x-1) == 0.
Subsets: loop mask from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1; bit i set means include item i.

topics.revision_note_md:
## Pattern matching

- Naive search: O(n·m).
- **KMP** precomputes the longest prefix that is also a suffix (LPS) to skip re-checking → O(n + m).
- **Z-function** gives, for each position, the length of the match with the prefix.

lesson.simple: Searching a word inside a long text naively restarts after every mismatch. KMP remembers how much of the pattern still matches, so it never moves backwards in the text.
key_points: Build the LPS array for the pattern.
On mismatch, jump j = lps[j-1] instead of restarting.
Concatenate pattern + '#' + text for Z-function matching.
Rolling hash (Rabin–Karp) is another linear-average approach.
